OUR BUSINESS AT A GLANCE

Our purpose is to

create enduring
mancoewenem WOT

Investec is a distinctive bank and wealth manager,
driven by commitment to our purpose, values, core
philosophies and culture. We deliver exceptional
service to our clients in the areas of banking and wealth
management, striving to create long-term value for

all our stakeholders and contributing meaningfully

to our people, communities and the planet.

Investec Group’s distinction

The Investec distinction is embodied in our entrepreneurial culture,
supported by a strong risk management discipline, client-centric approach
and an ability to be nimble, flexible and innovative. We do not seek to

be all things to all people. Our aim is to build well-defined, value-adding
businesses focused on serving the needs of select market niches where
we can compete effectively and build scale and relevance.

Our unique positioning is reflected in our iconic brand, our high-touch
and high-tech approach and our positive contribution to society, macro-
economic stability and the environment. Ours is a culture that values
purposeful thinking and stimulates extraordinary performance. We take
pride in the strength of our leadership tearm and our people are
empowered and committed to our values and culture.

OVERVIEW OF THE INVESTEC GROUP’S AND INVESTEC BANK PLC’S

ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE

Investec Bank plc (IBP) is the main banking subsidiary of Investec plc.

During July 2002, Investec Group Limited (since renamed Investec Limited) implemented a dual listed companies (DLC) structure

and listed its offshore business on the London Stock Exchange (LSE).

In terms of our DLC structure, Investec Limited is the holding company of the Investec Group’s businesses in Southern Africa, and
Investec plc is the holding company of Investec Group’s non-Southern African businesses. Investec Limited is listed on the
Johannesburg Stock Exchange Limited (JSE) South Africa (since 1986) and Investec plc on the LSE (since 2002).

All references in this report to the Bank, IBP or the Group relate to Investec Bank pic and its subsidiaries, whereas references to
Investec, Investec Group or DLC relate to the combined DLC Group comprising Investec pic and Investec Limited.

Acircular on the establishment of our DLC structure was issued on 20 June 2002 and is available on our website.

Maintained a sound balance sheet

The involvement of executive management ensures stringent management of risk, capital and liquidity as set out below.

Capital management

Capital and leverage ratios remain sound, ahead of internal targets and regulatory requirements.

Investec Bank plc calculates capital requirements using the standardised approach under the Basel Ill framework, thus our
risk-weighted assets represent a large portion of our total assets.

We are comfortable with our Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio at 13.3% given our solid capital-lignt revenues, and with the
leverage ratio at 9.5%.

STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT

Listening to
and engaging
with our
stakeholders

The Board recognises the importance of
understanding and responding to the diverse needs
and expectations of the Investec Bank plc’s (IBP)
stakeholders in delivering sustainable long-term
value. The Board is committed to providing
meaningful, transparent, timely and accurate financial
and non-financial information to primary stakeholders,
enabling them to make meaningful assessments and
informed investment decisions.

In order to achieve these outcomes, the Board
addresses material matters of significant interest and
concern, highlighting key risks to which the business
is exposed and actions taken to mitigate them.

IBP is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Investec plc (refer
to operational structure on page 8) and as such has
one shareholder. The Investec Bank plc Board
communicates regularly with the Board of Investec
plc. Certain IBP engagements with its stakeholders
are performed on an Investec Group basis such as
maintenance of its website, investor relations activity
and environmental, social and governance (ESG)
engagement.

®

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Strong stakeholder relationships
are essential to the creation of
enduring worth.

We engage with stakeholders on
an ongoing basis to understand
their needs and perspectives.
Insights from these engagements
are incorporated into management
processes and are considered by
the Board in its oversight and

decision-making.

As a wholly-owned subsidiary of Investec
plc, we engage with stakeholders both
directly and, where appropriate, through
broader Investec Group platforms, including
investor relations, digital channels and
sustainability initiatives.

the directors have had regard to the matters set
out in Section 172(1), and forms the directors’
statement required under the Companies Act
2006. This statement also provides details of how
the directors have engaged with and had regard
to the interests of our key stakeholders.

Non-executive succession

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Context

During the year, the Board undertook a process to
appoint a new Chair of the Investec Bank ple (IBP)
Board, following John Reizenstein stepping down
as Chair, effective 29 January 2026. This decision
was critical to ensuring continuity of independent
leadership, strong governance, and sustained
stakeholder confidence.

Stakeholders considered in the decision:

ig

000 Our
CONN people

[--]
Our

a investors

Our
regulators

How were stakeholder interests considered?

To ensure a transparent and well-governed process,
the Board developed detailed candidate specifications
aligned to anticipated Board requirements,
underpinned by continuous review of Board
composition, skills and future needs.

Consideration was given to expectations regarding
independence, experience and fitness and propriety,
including alignment with regulatory frameworks, as well
as the need to maintain strong governance, market
confidence and effective oversight of strategy and risk.

In line with established succession planning processes,
the Board balanced the need for continuity and
institutional knowledge with the importance of
maintaining independence and introducing
complementary skills and perspectives.

This approach aligns with the Board’s commitment to
diversity and inclusivity, ensuring an unbiased selection
process that prioritises varied backgrounds and
perspectives to reflect and serve the diverse interests
of stakeholders.

25

Outcomes

Following a formal and rigorous selection process,
Vivek Ahuja was appointed as Chair of the IBP Board
and Chair of the IBP Nomination Committee effective
20 March 2026.

Having been appointed to the Board of Investec Bank
plc in March 2025, Vivek brings extensive international
financial services experience across banking and
private equity, further enhancing the Board’s expertise
and strategic capabilities. His appointment supports
effective oversight of strategy, risk and capital
allocation.

Vivek stepped down from membership of the IBP Audit
Committee, with effect from 29 January 2026, to
ensure governance clarity and independence.

The Bank remains committed to continuously reviewing
Board composition and recruitment priorities to ensure
an appropriate balance of skills, experience and
perspectives, supporting ongoing Board effectiveness
and alignment with the Bank’s strategic objectives.

Investec Bank plc’s adjusted operating profit decreased by 2.1% to £486.3 million for the year ended 31 March 2026

(2025: £496.8 million). This reflects a resilient performance in a volatile and lower-rate environment, where underlying franchise
momentum was counterbalanced by margin compression and continued strategic investment.

Net interest income
Net interest income decreased by 7.2% to £733.2 million (2025: £790.5 million). The benefit of a larger average loan book was
offset by the impact of lower average interest rates and margin compression from competitive pricing.

GC) For a further analysis of interest received and interest paid refer to page 150.

Net fee and commission income

Net fee and commission income increased by 14.5% to £206.6 million (2025: £180.5 million). This is reflective of higher
arrangement fees generated across our investment banking lending franchises, including strong deal activity in our Aviation
franchise.

GC) For a further analysis of net fee and commission income refer to page 150.

Investment income
Investment income of £42.9 million (2025: £41.8 million) was largely driven by net realised fair value movements from equity
investments and higher dividend income.

GC) For a further analysis of investment income refer to page 151.

Share of post-taxation profit of associates and joint venture holdings

Share of post-tax operating profit of associates and joint venture holdings amounted to £89.9 million (2025; £72.4 million) primarily
comprising Investec Bank plc's share of Rathbones’ post-tax underlying profit attributable to shareholders of £177.4 million for their
year ended 31 December 2025 which amounts to £76.6 million (2025: £69.1 million). We have accrued earnings at an average
effective interest of 43.15% for the year, taking into consideration the elimination of treasury shares held within Rathbones Group
and the impact of the Rathbones share buyback in the current year. In prior years, the consideration of treasury shares had not
been applied and earnings were accrued at 41.25%, as such an additional £4.3 million has been recognised in 1H2026 to account
for the differential.

Trading income

Trading income from customer flow increased to £91.5 million (2025: £85.5 million), underpinned by increased facilitation client
hedging activity by our Treasury Risk Solutions business.

Trading income from balance sheet management and other trading activities decreased to £6.0 million (2025: £14.2 million)
reflecting current period movements in hedging instruments used to manage the balance sheet.

Other operating income
Other operating income mainly reflects an insurance recovery from a previously written-off exposure.
Expected credit loss impairment charges

Total ECL impairment charges totalled £97.3 million (2025: £97.0 million), resulting in a credit loss ratio of 57bps (2025: 60bps).
ECL impairment charges in the current year were largely driven by Stage 3 ECL charges on certain exposures. We have seen no
evidence of trend deterioration in the overall credit quality of our books.

Stage 3 exposures remained stable at 3.4% of gross loans subject to ECL (2025: 3.4%). We have seen a reduction in exposures
migrating into Stage 3.

Refer to pages 244 for further information on asset quality and page 245 for a breakdown of the expected credit loss impairment
charges.

PRIVATE BANKING

Our Private Banking activities focus on providing bespoke solutions underpinned by in-depth knowledge and
understanding of our clients’ personal and business aspirations and goals, supported by a broad private banking
offering. We understand that every client is an individual, and that they are typically active wealth creators with

opportunity to address an underserved part of the UK market. This segment comprises lending (primarily
residential mortgages), savings and transactional banking (including international payments) to HNW clients,

It has always been central to Investec’s strategy to provide a coordinated banking and wealth management offering. Prior to the
combination with Rathbones, IW&l UK was consistently one of the leading private client wealth managers in the UK and a highly
respected franchise in the industry.

On 23 September 2023 an all-share combination of IW&l UK and Rathbones was completed, resulting in the Investec Group owning
a 41.25% economic interest in the combined Rathbones Group, and creating the Uk’s leading discretionary wealth manager.
Rathbones Group reported FUMA of £113.6 billion as at 31 March 2026.

The combination brought together two reputable UK wealth management businesses with closely aligned cultures and operating
models and established a long-term, strategic partnership which enhances the client proposition across banking and wealth
management services for both groups. The combination represents a significant value-creation trajectory for all stakeholders.

In the current and prior year the Group's investment in Rathbones has been equity accounted for and recognised as an associate.

RISK MANAGEMENT APPROACH AND FRAMEWORK

Information provided in this section of the annual report is
prepared on an Investec Bank plc (IBP) consolidated basis
unless otherwise stated.

Philosophy and approach to risk
management

The Bank's comprehensive risk management process involves
identifying, quantifying, managing, monitoring, mitigating and
reporting the risks associated with each of the businesses to
ensure the risks remain within the stated risk appetite.

The Board ensures that there are appropriate resources to
manage the risks arising from running our businesses.

The {BP Board Risk and Capital Committee (IBP BRCC)
(comprising both executive and non-executive directors) is the
Board mandated committee to monitor and oversee risk. IBP
BRCC meets four to six times per annum and recommends the
overall risk appetite to the Board for approval.

We monitor and control risk exposure through independent
credit, market, liquidity, operational, legal, internal audit, capital
and compliance teams. This approach is core to assuming a
tolerable risk and reward profile, helping us to pursue controlled
growth across our business.

Risk management operates within an integrated geographical
and divisional structure, in line with our management approach,
ensuring that the appropriate processes are used to address all
risks across the Bank. There are specialist divisions in the UK
and smaller risk divisions in other regions tasked with promoting
sound risk management practices.

Risk management units are locally responsive yet globally
aware. This helps to ensure that all initiatives and businesses
operate within our defined risk parameters and objectives.
We continually seek new ways to enhance risk

management techniques.

We believe that the risk management systems and processes
we have in place are adequate to support the Bank's strategy
and allow the Bank to operate within its risk appetite tolerance.

Risk management objectives are to:
e Ensure adherence to our risk management culture

* Support the long-term sustainability of the Bank by providing
an established, independent framework for identifying,
evaluating, monitoring and mitigating risk with good customer
outcomes

¢ Set, approve and monitor adherence to underlying risk
parameters and limits across the Bank and ensure they
are implemented and adhered to consistently within the
Board-approved risk appetite

+ Aggregate and monitor exposure across risk classes

Maintain compliance in relation to regulatory requirements

Coordinate risk management activities across the Bank,
covering all legal entities and jurisdictions

Establish and convene appropriate risk committees, as
mandated by the relevant Boards

« Resource risk teams suitably and with appropriate expertise
and facilitate operating independence

Provide the IBP Board reasonable assurance that the risks the
Bank is exposed to are identified and appropriately managed
and controlled.

Risk management framework, committees
and forums

A number of committees and forums identify and manage risk
at a Bank level, as shown in the diagram below. These
committees and forums operate together with risk management
and are mandated by the IBP Board. Any matters relevant to IBP
are communicated to the Bank, in part, through having one or
more directors of Investec Group as members of the Board
committees of the Bank.

YEAR IN REVIEW FROM A RISK PERSPECTIVE

A summary of the year in review from a risk
perspective

The executive management is integrally involved in ensuring
stringent management of risk through our risk appetite
framework, and embedding a culture of risk consciousness
in all staff. The risk appetite framework is set taking into
consideration prevailing market conditions and the Bank’s
strategy. The primary aim is to achieve a suitable balance
between risk and reward in our businesses.

Despite ongoing geopolitical tensions across the world,
including the latest conflict in the Middle East, we have
continued to grow our business in a risk conscious manner and
are well placed to navigate the uncertainty. The Bank has
operated against a backdrop of ongoing global market volatility,
including uncertainty in equity valuations, developments in
private credit markets, currency fluctuations and changes in
forward-looking interest rate, inflation and energy cost
assumptions. Notwithstanding these conditions, the Bank has
performed strongly and is well positioned to benefit from
emerging opportunities.

The Bank remains well capitalised, maintains high levels of
liquidity, runs modest levels of market risk and favours secured
lending to clients with predictable income streams.

Loans and advances to customers as a percentage of customer
deposits remained conservative at 79.0% (31 March 2025:
78.0%). The Bank has a substantial portion of eligible deposits
that are covered by Financial Services Compensation Scheme
(FSCS) protection, We have limited reliance on wholesale
funding but we maintain access and presence, using wholesale
issuance to strategically diversify our funding base and
complement the other liability channels by focusing, where
appropriate, on tenor and currency as part of a longer term
strategic plan.

The Minimum Requirements for Own Funds and Eligible
Liabitities (MREL) transition has commenced from

1 January 2026 in a phased manner with end-state MREL
applying from 1 January 2032. Investec plc resolution status
with respect to MREL changed to bail-in from 1 January 2026.
In the year ahead, a Key priority is the completion of its
Recoverability Assessment Framework (RAF). This will further
strengthen the Group's recovery and resolution framework and
will be delivered alongside planned issuance activity.

Cash and near cash balances at 31 March 2026 amounted

to £9.4 billion (31 March 2025: £9.1 billion). We maintain a high
level of readily available, high-quality liquid assets (HQLA),
targeting a minimum cash to customer deposit ratio of 25%.
Current cash and near cash is equivalent to 41.6% of customer
deposits (31 March 2025: 42.2%). At 31 March 2026, on an IBP
solo basis, the Liquidity Coverage ratio (LCR) was 348% and
Net Stable Funding ratio (NSFR) was 140%, both metrics well
ahead of current minimum regulatory requirements.

We continue to maintain a structural hedging programme in the
UK to reduce sensitivity of earnings to interest rate movements.

The Bank's focus remains on maintaining a strong liquidity
position as we continue to navigate global markets with
heightened levels of volatility.

IBP’s long-term Moody's deposit rating is A1 (stable outlook)
and during the year Investec pic's rating was upgraded one
notch to A3 (stable outlook), which will continue to support
MREL issuance. IBP’s long-term Fitch issuer default rating
remains at A- (stable outlook).

We have successfully grown our loan book while ensuring its
resilience and remaining focused on our core areas of
expertise. Competitive pressures have increased across our
markets, including from private credit participants, however the
Bank continues to operate within its defined risk appetite and
maintains a disciplined approach to underwriting and risk
selection.

We are strategically positioned to pursue disciplined growth
and have strong levels of capital and liquidity to support such
growth. Increased and diversified client activity and new client
acquisition resulted in an increase in the Bank's net core loan
book to £17.8 billion (31 March 2025: £16.8 billion). Growth was
due to increased activity diversified across multiple asset
classes of corporate client lending as well as residential
mortgage lending.

Credit exposures are focused on secured lending to a select
target market, comprising high-income and high net worth
individuals, established corporates and medium-sized
enterprises, Our risk appetite continued to favour lower risk,
income~based lending, with exposures well collateralised and
with credit risk taken over a short to medium term. We remain
focused on our target market, supporting clients with significant
wealth and experience in their chosen sectors, as indicated by
our continued growth in the private banking space as we
execute on our strategy to target this sector of the market.
Over the past few years we have realigned and rebalanced
our portfolios in line with our risk appetite framework and this
is reflected in the movements in asset classes on our balance
sheet; showing an increase in private client, mortgages and
corporate and other lending, and maintaining lending
collateralised by property as a proportion of net core loans.

Concentration risk is well managed and exposures are spread
across geographies and industries. We remain confident that
we have a well-diversified portfolio across sectors.

The Bank‘s net core loan exposures remain well diversified
with commercial rent producing property loans comprising
approximately 7.8% of net core loans, other lending
collateralised by property 6.2%, high net worth and other
private client lending 35.0% and corporate and other lending
51.0% (with most industry concentrations well below 5%).

Asset quality ratios reflect the solid performance of the
underlying portfolios despite challenging conditions. The credit
loss ratio reduced to 0.57% at 31 March 2026 (31 March 2025:
0.60%), in line with guidance provided in November 2025. This
was driven by specific idiosyncratic impairments, in part given
higher for longer rates and challenges in achieving anticipated
exit valuations.

Stage 3 remained flat at 3.4% of gross core loans subject to

exposures remain diversified across multiple asset classes and
provisions are individually assessed.

Stage 2 exposures as a proportion of gross core loans subject
to ECL decreased to 7.4% at 31 March 2026 (31 March 2025:
8.1%) as underlying portfolios continue to perform.

The measurement of ECL under IFRS 9 creates reliance on
expert credit judgements. Key judgemental areas under IFRS 9
are highlighted in this document and are subject to robust
governance processes. Stage 3 ECLs continue to be assessed
using a combination of scenario analysis, expert judgement and
modelled ECL.

PRINCIPAL RISKS

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Principal risks are the most material and significant risks we face, which
the Board and senior management believe could have an impact on our
strategy, operations, financial performance and viability. These risks are
summarised in the section that follows, with further information
pertaining to the management and monitoring thereof.

Risk appetite

The Bank has a number of Board-approved risk appetite
statements and policy documents covering our risk appetite
and approach to our principal aspects of risk. The risk appetite
framework and statement set out the Board’s mandated risk
appetite. The risk appetite framework acts as a guide to
determine the acceptable risk profile of the Bank while keeping
in line with the Investec Group's risk appetite parameters. The
risk appetite statement ensures that limits/targets are applied
and monitored across all key operating jurisdictions and legal
entities.

The risk appetite framework is a function of business strategy,
budget and capital processes, our stress testing reviews and
the regulatory and economic environment in which the Bank is
operating. The risk appetite framework is reviewed (in light of
the above aspects) and approved by the Board at least annually
or as business needs dictate.

A documented process exists where our risk profile is measured
against our risk appetite and this positioning is presented to the
IBP BRCC and Board as well as the DLC BRCC and DLC Board.
In the section that follows, the Bank's high-level summary of
overall risk appetite and positioning has been detailed against
the respective principal risks.

Three levels of defence

The Bank has a strong and embedded risk and capital
management culture with policies, processes and systems
in place to address these principal risks. Risk awareness,
governance, controls and compliance are embedded in all
our day-to-day activities through a levels of defence model.

The levels of defence model is applied as follows:

* Level 1~ Business units: responsible for identifying and
managing risks inherent in the products, activities, processes

and systems for which they are accountable

Level 2 ~Independent risk and compliance functions:
responsible for building and embedding risk frameworks,
monitoring the implementation of effective risk management
practices, challenging the business lines’ inouts to, and
outputs from, the Bank's risk management, risk measurement
and reporting activities

Level 3 ~ Independent internal audit: responsible for
providing independent and objective assurance over the
design and effectiveness of governance, risk management
and control processes.

47

Overview of principal risks

The Board, through its various committees, has performed a
robust assessment of the principal risks and regular reporting
of these risks is made to the Board.

The Board recognises that, even with sound appetite and
judgement, extreme events can occur which are outside of its
control. It is, therefore, necessary to assess these potential
events and possible mitigating actions. It is the Bank's policy to
regularly conduct multiple stress testing scenarios (including
reverse stress testing) which, in theory, test extreme but
plausible events and from that, assess and plan what can be
done to mitigate the potential outcomes.

In addition to the principal risks, emerging risks continue to be
reviewed and assessed. These emerging risks are evaluated for
their inherent risk level and potential impact on the Bank's
strategy, operations, financial performance and viability.
Mitigation measures are considered to address these emerging
risks, taking into account their potential influence on the
principal risks.

A number of these risks are beyond the Bank's control and are
considered in our capital plans, stress testing analyses and
budget processes, where applicable.

The Bank's stress testing framework is well embedded in its
operations and is designed to identify and regularly test the
Bank's key vulnerabilities under stress. A fundamental part of
the stress testing process is a full and comprehensive analysis
of the Bank's material business activities, incorporating views
from risk, the business units and the executive - a process
called the ‘bottom-up’ analysis. Resulting from the ‘bottom-up’
analysis, the Investec-specific stress scenarios are designed to
specifically test the unique attributes of the Bank's portfolio.
The key is to understand the potential threats to our
sustainability and profitability and thus a number of risk
scenarios are developed and assessed.

These stress scenarios form an integral part of our capital
planning process and IFRS 9 reporting. The stress testing
process also informs the risk appetite review process and the
management of risk appetite limits and is a key risk
management tool of the Bank. Reverse stress tests are
conducted to stress the Bank’s business plan to failure and
consider a broad variety of extreme and remote events. These
processes allow the Bank to proactively identify underlying risks
and manage them accordingly.

liabilities into variable rate items

BRCC) is responsible for the oversight and management of capital and leverage

The leverage ratio is considered and monitored as part of the capital management framework

A detailed assessment of the regulatory and internat capital position is undertaken on an annual
basis and is documented in the ICAAP. The ICAAP is prepared at the consolidated Investec plc level
and incorporates the Bank (solo-consolidation basis)*. The document is reviewed by the IBP, PLC
and DLC Capital Committees before being recommended for approval to the IBP BRCC, DLC BRCC
and the IBP and DLC Boards.

Risk appetite and tolerance metric

We intend to maintain a sufficient level of capital to
satisfy regulatory requirements and our internal target
ratios. We target a Total Capital ratio range

of between 14% and 17%, a minimum Tier 1 ratio of
>11% and a CET1 ratio of >10%, on a salo-
consolidated and consolidated basis for IBP.

We maintain a conservative leverage profile and
target a leverage ratio in excess of 6%.

Positioning at 31 March 2026
The Bank met all these targets.

IBP applies the provisions laid down in article 9 of the CRR (solo-consolidation waiver) and therefore includes Investec Investments (UK) Limited in the solo-

consolidation basis.

CHAIR'S INTRODUCTION

Vivek Ahuja
Chair

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

The Bank has delivered a resilient
performance in a more demanding
environment, while continuing to invest for
long-term growth and strengthen the
alignment of activities across the Group

Introduction

The year under review has been one of disciplined execution
against a more demanding external backdrop. The Board’s
focus has remained firmly on the safe and sustainable delivery
of the Bank’s strategy, the strength of its capital, liquidity and
risk profile, and effective oversight of the matters most material
to the Bank’s long-term performance.

John Reizenstein stepped down as Chair during the year
following a formal Chair succession process, concluding his
tenure on 29 January 2026. Following receipt of regulatory
approval, | assumed the role of Chair on 20 March 2026. The
Board thanks John for his contribution during his tenure.
Continuity in governance, oversight and strategic direction has
been maintained throughout the transition.

This report sets out how the Board has discharged its
responsibilities over the period — its oversight of performance,
strategy and risk, the priorities it has progressed during the
year, its engagement with stakeholders, and its assessment of
its own effectiveness.

Performance

The Bank delivered a resilient financial performance against a
challenging macroeconomic backdrop, characterised by modest
UK growth, easing but still elevated inflation, a normalising
interest rate cycle and continued geopolitical tension. Operating
performance has been supported by the strength and diversity
of the Bank’s client franchises, with growth in fee income,
customer-flow trading and the contribution from associates
helping to offset the impact of lower net interest income as the
interest rate environment normalised.

The Bank has continued to invest for long-term growth, with
sustained momentum in lending and customer deposit
gathering supporting its diversified client franchises. Capital and
liquidity positions remained strong, and credit quality continued
to be sound. This outcome is a testament to our people, the
strength of the Bank's client franchises and to management's
measured approach in navigating margin pressures, while
maintaining cost discipline, strong liquidity and conservative
capital buffers, alongside continued investment in the Bank's
strategic priorities.

Further detail on the Bank’s financial
performance is set out on pages 11 to 15.

62

Board leadership and culture

The Board's role is to ensure the Bank is governed effectively,
operates within a clear risk framework, and delivers sustainable
outcomes for its clients, its people, its shareholders and the
wider stakeholders it serves. Throughout the year, the Non-
Executive Directors have exercised independent oversight and
provided constructive challenge to management on strategy,
performance, risk, controls and culture.

The tone set by the Board continues to reflect Investec’s
purpose, culture and values, and its long-standing commitment
to client-centricity, integrity and disciplined growth. The Board
has reinforced its expectation that these values are embedded
consistently across the Group and reflected in how the Bank
operates as a cohesive global organisation, and has supported
the continued strengthening of alignment, collaboration and
consistency across the Group.

Board priorities and areas of focus

During the year, the Board’s work has centred on the disciplined
delivery of strategy, the oversight of financial performance and
risk, and the effective progression of a substantive governance
and regulatory agenda. The Board has supported management
in investing for long-term growth, including the continued
development of the Bank's client franchises and progression of
key growth initiatives across Corporate Mid-Market and Private
Client, while maintaining close scrutiny of margin pressures,
revenue visibility and capital allocation in the context ofa .
normalising rate cycle.

In a More uncertain external environment, the Board has
remained focused on the Bank's resilience, maintaining strong
capital and liquidity positions and overseeing progress towards
the Internal Ratings Based (IRB) approach. It has also overseen
key regulatory programmes, including resolvability and
operational resilience, alongside the ongoing implementation of
Provision 29 of the UK Corporate Governance Code 2024 (the
Code).

Implementation of the UK Corporate
Governance Code 2024

The Board has dedicated significant time during the year to
preparing the Bank for the revised Code, with particular focus
on enhancing the Bank’s risk management and internal control
framework in anticipation of the requirements of Provision 29.
This work has formed part of the Board’s broader consideration
of effective governance, accountability and oversight under the
revised Code. It remains ongoing, and the Board continues to
monitor delivery against the implementation plan to ensure the
Bank is well positioned to meet the new requirements when
they become applicable.

Stakeholder engagement

The Board remains committed to the Bank’s responsibilities to
its stakeholders and the importance of operating in line with
Investec’s purpose, culture and values. These principles
underpin how the Bank engages with its stakeholders and
support the long-term relationships and sustainable outcomes
that are central to the Bank’s strategy.

During the year, the Board has continued to oversee how these
principles are embedded in decision-making and reflected in
the way the Bank supports its clients, develops and engages its
people, and conducts its business responsibly. This reflects
investec’s long-standing philosophy of operating as a purpose-
led organisation, with a clear recognition that its success is
closely linked to the broader environment in which it operates.

Engagement with the Bank's regulators, including the Prudential
Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority, has
been maintained throughout the year by the Committee Chairs
and Executive Directors - supporting transparency, forward
visibility of supervisory priorities and constructive dialogue with
the Bank’s principal regulators.

Investec Bank ple Annual Financial Statements 2026

Board performance and effectiveness

Delivering on the responsibilities and priorities described above
requires an effective and well-functioning Board. The Board has
therefore continued to assess its performance and
effectiveness during the year.

During the year, the Board undertook an internally facilitated
evaluation of its performance, following on from the externally
facilitated review completed in the prior year. This approach
reflects the Board’s established evaluation cycle, under which
an externally led review is conducted at least every three years,
consistent with the requirements of the Code.

The Board concluded that it was operating effectively. The
review identified opportunities to deepen strategic debate,
strengthen oversight of growth initiatives and continue Board
development. An action plan has been agreed and will be
monitored throughout the year.

Further detail is set out in the Nomination
Committee report on pages 75 and 78.

Looking ahead

Looking ahead, the Board remains focused on supporting
disciplined growth and sustainable returns, while preserving the
Bank's strong capital and liquidity position. In an evolving
economic and regulatory environment, this will require
continued careful oversight of balance sheet strength, capital
allocation and risk, with a clear emphasis on long-term value
creation.

The Board will also oversee the phased implementation of the
Code, including further enhancement of the Bank's risk
management and internal control framework in preparation for
Provision 29. Maintaining a robust and proportionate control
environment, capable of responding to emerging risks, will
remain a key priority.

Operational and technological resilience will continue to be
areas of focus, supported by ongoing investment in technology
modernisation, data and reporting capabilities, and the
resilience of critical services. These efforts are intended to
support the Bank’s growth ambitions and the experience of its
clients and its people.

The Board will continue to prioritise succession planning and
Board capability, ensuring that the composition of the Board
and executive leadership evolves in line with the Bank's
strategic direction and operating environment. This includes a
continued focus on skills, experience and diversity to support
effective challenge and decision-making.

The Board remains confident in the Bank's strategy, culture and
leadership. The Board and | thank our people for their continued
dedication, and our stakeholders for their ongoing trust and
support.

COMPLIANCE WITH THE UK CORPORATE GOVERNANCE CODE

The UK Corporate Governance Code 2024 (2024 Code) applied to the Bank for the financial year ended 31 March 2026, with the
exception of Provision 29 which applies to the Bank’s financial year which begins on 1 April 2026. The Bank will report against
Provision 29 of the 2024 Code in its annual report and accounts for the year ending 31 March 2027. Provision 29 of the UK
Corporate Governance Code 2018 (2018 Code) applied to the financial year ended 31 March 2026. The Board confirms that the
Bank applied the principles and complied with the relevant provisions of the 2024 Code, together with Provision 29 of the 2018
Code, throughout the financial year, with the exception of Provision 12 (Senior Independent Director), for which an explanation is
provided. The table below is designed to help stakeholders evaluate how this has been achieved. A copy of the 2024 Code is
publicly available on the Financial Reporting Council's website: www.frc.org.uk.

Board leadership and Company purpose

A. An effective entrepreneurial Board, collectively accountable for the
long-term sustainable success of the Bank, generating value for
shareholders and contributing to wider society (see pages 64 to
66 for directors’ biographies)

B. Purpose, values and strategy are aligned with culture, which is
promoted by the Board. Further details are available on page 4

C. In line with Principle C of the 2024 Code, governance reporting
focusses on the Board’s decisions, and the outcomes of these
decisions in the context of the Bank’s strategy and objectives. The
Board does not depart from the Code’s provisions. However, if it
were to do so, it would provide a clear explanation

D. Engagement with the Bank's stakeholders is effective and
encourages their participation (see pages 16 to 25 for more
information)

E. Workforce policies and practices are consistent with the Bank's

and are overseen by the Board. The workforce is able to raise

Non-compliance with Provision 12

The Board recognises the requirement for a Senior Independent Director (SID). The Nomination Committee reaffirmed its decision
not to appoint one and has provided an explanation in accordance with the ‘comply or explain’ framework of the 2024 Code.

While the Board notes the Code requirement for a SID, it is satisfied that appropriate and effective alternative arrangements are in
place, consistent with the Group's governance structure and culture. It is noted that under the Code, the key responsibilities of the
SID are to provide a sounding board for the Chair, to serve as an intermediary for the other directors and shareholders, and to
appraise the Chairs performance. Given the structure of the Investec Group, in particular the cross-directorships between the
Boards and committees and our culture, we believe that there are sufficient communication channels open for directors. There are
existing communication channels available to the Bank Chair from a sounding board perspective, and for other directors and the
shareholders and the Investec Group, from an intermediary perspective. This further aligns with the process adopted by the Investec
Group's other principal subsidiaries, which do not have SIDs. The assessment of the Chair's performance will be conducted by the
Chair of the Investec Group.

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Strategy

Strategic initiatives

The Board oversaw the delivery of the Bank's strategic
priorities, including the continued development of its client
franchises and growth initiatives across core markets, while
maintaining close scrutiny of performance across the
business, with particular attention to margin pressures,
revenue visibility and capital allocation.

71

Financial

Budget

The Board considered performance versus the 2025/26 budget.

The Board approved the budget for the year ending 31 March
2027, recognising the continuation of investment required to
deliver strategic initiatives. The Board discussed key assumptions
and delivery risks, the need to maintain capital discipline in a
competitive and margin-pressured environment, and the
importance of supporting long-term growth through continued
investment while preserving a diversified and resilient revenue
base.

Going concern and viability statement

The Board reviewed in detail and approved the Going Concern
and Viability Statements, following rigorous assessment of the
underlying assumptions, financial forecasts and stress-testing
scenarios,

In reaching its conclusions, the Board considered the Bank's
capital and liquidity position, projected profitability, principal risks
and severe but plausible downside scenarios, drawing on analysis
presented by management and challenged by the Audit and Risk
Committees. The Board satisfied itself that the forecasts were
appropriately prudent, that sensitivities had been robustly
modelled, and that mitigating actions were credible and within
management's control.

Through this process, the Board ensured that the Going Concern
and Viability Statements are supported by a sound evidential
basis and provide transparent assurance to shareholders and
other stakeholders regarding the Bank's resilience, financial
sustainability and long-term prospects.

Results

The Board reviewed and approved the full year results.

Risk and assurance

Risk profile

The Board reviewed and debated the overall risk
profile, particularly the principal risks, emerging
tisks and risk appetite. The Board approved the
risk appetite ensuring there was adequate
diversification, reducing concentration and
country risk while enabling the Bank to achieve
its strategic objective of growth. The Board
continued to monitor and challenge the risk
profile of the Bank, respanding to the ongoing
macro-economic environment by focusing on the
key financial risks, in particular liquidity, market
risk and credit quality.

Risk management

In line with the Board’s ongoing responsibilities under the Code, the Board undertook a comprehensive review of the Bank's risk management
systems, including financial, operational and compliance controls. The Board assessed the robustness and effectiveness of the Bank's key internal
contro! systems, ensuring that they are designed and operated to identify, manage and mitigate risks appropriately. This process included regular
monitoring and evaluation to ensure controls remain fit for purpose in a changing risk environment, providing assurance that the Bank is able to
tespond effectively to emerging risks and maintain sound governance standards.

Provision 29 of the 2024 UK Corporate Governance Code will apply to the Bank’s annual report for the financial year ending 31 March 2027. This
requirement will therefore first be reported against in the Bank’s next annual report, covering FY27. During the year under review, the Board
commenced a structured implementation programme to ensure full compliance with the new requirements, including preparing for the enhanced
Board declaration on the effectiveness of risk management and internal control systems. The Board retains overall accountability for the
programme. The Audit Committee and Risk Committee have played a central role in overseeing delivery, including reviewing the project plan,
monitoring progress against key milestones and challenging management's assessment of control effectiveness, assurance mapping and
documentation standards. The Committees have provided regular updates to the Board to ensure collective oversight and alignment as the
programme progresses towards FY27 readiness.

Extemal advisers have been engaged to support the Board in benchmarking the Bank's framework against emerging market practice, assessing the
maturity of existing controls, and advising on evidencing the effectiveness review in a manner consistent with regulatory and investor
expectations.

In March 2026, Directors participated in a dedicated development session focused on the practical implications of Provision 29, including the
scope of the Board declaration, the evidential threshold required, and the interaction with existing ICAAP, ILAAP, recovery and resolution, and
Internal audit assurance processes. This session was designed to ensure the Board is fully equipped to discharge its responsibilities and to provide
arobust and defensible effectiveness statement in the 2027 annual report.

The implementation programme is intended not only to achieve technical compliance, but to strengthen the Bank's control environment, clarify
accountability and enhance transparency. By formalising the Board's assessment of control effectiveness, the Bank reinforces disciplined risk
management, supports resilient decision-making and provides greater assurance to shareholders, customers, regulators and employees that risks
are being identified and managed in a structured and proportionate manner. This work also supports the Board's oversight of a consistent,
evidence-based view of control effectiveness across the Bank, enhancing the quality of governance, decision-making and stakeholder confidence.

Secretary, prepared a self-assessment questionnaire, which
was distributed to all the directors for completion. The
questionnaire sought the directors’ views on a range of topics
including performance and effectiveness of the Board and its
committees, composition, strategy and, culture.

opportunity to raise any other matters.

Stage 3: A report was prepared, based on the results of the

discussed with the Chair, whose feedback was incorporated
into a final discussion paper including the proposed action plan.

Stage 4: The final report was presented to the 8oard in March
2026, following its consideration by the Committee.

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

The Committee has continued to monitor

Introduction

| am pleased to present the report of the IBP Audit Committee
(the Committee) for the financial year ended 31 March 2026.

The Committee continued its focus on the key accounting
judgements, providing challenge to management when
required. This work underpins transparent and robust financial
reporting, supporting informed decision-making and the
Group’s focus on investing for long-term growth. Of particular
note were the assumptions underpinning the expected credit
loss (ECL) calculations and models, including forward-looking
macro-economic scenarios and weightings. The valuations of
level 3 instruments were subject to scrutiny and challenge,
reflecting increased subjectivity in the current geopolitical
environment and a number of technical accounting matters in
the financial year were debated with management and Deloitte
including the accounting treatment of acquisitions relating to
the Bank's operations in Switzerland, certain aviation
transactions and the treatment of technology and restructuring
costs. The Committee also reviewed the use of alternative
profit measures, the findings raised by Deloitte and other
judgemental items in the financial statements.

The Committee considered the impact of heightened
geopolitical tensions in the Middle East on the Bank's financial
reporting judgements, including ECLs, valuations, and going
concern and liquidity assumptions. The Committee reviewed
management's scenario analysis, challenged the
reasonableness of key assumptions and sensitivities, and
concluded that the related disclosures appropriately reflected
the current level of uncertainty.

During the year, the FCA published its redress scheme relating
to motor vehicle finance. As previously advised, the Bank has
an exposure to this industry through the Mann Island business
and the Committee debated the appropriateness of the Bank’s
provision. Following the FCA’s final announcement on the
industry-wide motor finance commission redress scheme in
March 2026, management reassessed the financial impact
across all in-scope agreements. The Committee challenged
management's assumptions underpinning this provision, and
was satisfied that it remains appropriate, reflecting updated
assumptions on eligibility, redress methodology, take-up rates
and operational costs. The FCA’s scheme is subject to ongoing

79

legal challenges which, if successful, may materially affect the
design, implementation or existence of any redress framework.
The tegal and regulatory position, as well as the nature, extent
and timing of any remediation, remain materially uncertain
pending the outcome of this challenge. Accordingly, the
Committee reviewed the adequacy and clarity of disclosures
on this matter to ensure that the uncertainty had been
appropriately reflected.

Further details of the key accounting issues considered by the
Committee are set out on the following pages.

The Committee oversaw work in relation to Provision 29 of the
FRC’s UK Corporate Governance Code 2024 (the Code), which
introduces a future Board declaration on the effectiveness of
material controls. Although the dectaration will not apply until
the financial year ending 31 March 2027, the Committee has
supported early implementation activity, including
management updates on the controls framework, work to
identify material controls, and director training delivered

with Ernst & Young.

The Committee received regular reports from Internal Audit on
the delivery of key regulatory programmes, including the
Resolvability Assessment Framework (RAF) and the Internal
Ratings Based (IRB) model programme, providing independent
assurance over progress, governance and contro!
effectiveness. Reports were also received on regulatory
reporting. During the year, the Committee also participated in
joint sessions with the DLC Audit Committee, which included
the evaluation of internal and external audit effectiveness and
presentations on the increasing use of data analytics across
the audit and risk environment, developments in ECL
modelling, and progress made to incorporate climate-related
risk considerations within the Bank’s models. These sessions
supported effective oversight, consistency of approach across
the Investec Group, and the Committee's understanding of
emerging modelling and data-driven risks, reflecting Investec’s
operation as a globally connected group rather than a
segmented or isolated entity.

How the Audit Committee works

The Committee exercises authority delegated by the Investec
Bank pic Board in accordance with the Code, the Companies

Act 2006 and applicable PRA and FCA requirements. The IBP

Audit Committee's principal responsibilities are to:

« Monitor the integrity of the Bank's financial reporting and
satisfy itself, having regard to any issues raised by the
external auditor, as to the appropriateness of management's
accounting policies and practices

Assess that any significant financial judgements,
assumptions or estimates made and the disclosures
recommended by management are appropriate and whether
overall the annual report, taken as a whole, is fair, balanced
and understandable; and provides the information necessary
for stakeholders to assess the Bank's position and
performance, business model and strategy

Composition, meeting attendance, and interaction
with Investec Group

In accordance with the Code, the Committee entirely
comprises independent non-executive directors who meet
predetermined skills, competency and experience
requirements as determined by the IBP Nomination
Committee.

Members’ continuing independence, as well as their required
skills, competencies and experience is assessed annually. The
Committee’s composition and experience enable robust
challenge of management and auditors.

The CEO and Finance Director of the Bank attend meetings on
a regular basis but are not members. Other Bank directors may
also attend by invitation. The Head of Risk, Head of Internal
Audit, the external auditor and the Company Secretary also
attend meetings on a regular basis.

The Committee meets alone with the external auditor and,
separately, with the Head of Internal Audit. Committee
members also meet periodically with management and the
Heads of Internal Audit, Operational and IT risk, and Finance as
well as the lead external audit partner and senior management
in order to keep knowledge up to date, and to keep abreast of
commercial developments and challenges facing the business.

The Chair of the Committee is also a member of the IBP BRCC
and, similarly, the Chair of IBP BRCC, Paul Seward, is a
member of this Committee. This reciprocity of membership
helps to ensure interaction between these two committees
and a coordinated consideration of the Bank's risks and
internal controls where they overlap in relation to both financial
risks and non-financial risks, reflecting the holistic oversight of
risk at Board level.

The Committee reports formally to the Board.

Diane Radley Chair of the DLC Audit Committees, is also a
member of this Committee. This appointment reflects the dual-
listed structure of the Investec Group in which Investec Bank
pic is the principal banking subsidiary in the UK and the parent
company of other material overseas subsidiaries. The
representation of the Investec Group Audit Committee Chair
ensures that Key audit matters for the Bank and its subsidiaries
are visible at the Investec Group level, and likewise that key
audit matters and matters of mutual interest for the Investec
Group and Investec Bank plc are communicated and
addressed, where applicable, in the Bank and its subsidiaries.

The Committee has provided robust
oversight of the Bank’s risk profile and is
satisfied that its risk and control
frameworks are effective and aligned with
regulatory expectations.

Introduction

| am pleased to present the report on how the IBP BRCC (the
Committee) has discharged its responsibilities during the year.

The Committee continues to monitor and challenge the risk
profile of the Bank with particular focus on its evolving financial
and non-financial risk profile through a period of heightened
regulatory activity, continued macro-economic uncertainty and
material change across the business. This oversight supports
the Bank's focus on investing for long-term growth while
maintaining a prudent and resilient risk profile. During the
period under review, the Committee oversaw the Bank's risk
position as inflation remained above target, interest rate
reductions moderated and pressures across credit markets
persisted. The Committee continued to challenge management
over credit quality, liquidity positioning and market-risk
exposures, noting that financial risk metrics remained strong
throughout the year.

Due to the heightened geopolitical uncertainty, the Committee
undertook dynamic reviews of certain risk exposures during the
year. This included out-of-cycle deep-dive sessions, outside the
Committee's usual forward work plan, to consider emerging
risks and potential impacts. !n particular, the Committee
received detailed analysis on the potential implications of tariff
developments and trade-related measures, as weil as focused
updates on the evolving situation in the Middle East and the
possible consequences for the Bank’s risk profile. These
discussions supported the Committee's ongoing oversight of
emerging risks and the resilience of the Bank’s risk management
framework, within the context of Investec operating as a
globally connected group.

The Committee monitored closely the industry-wide Motor
finance review, receiving regular updates on evolving FCA
proposals, provision adequacy and data-validation activity,
consistent with the Committee’s responsibilities to monitor
emerging conduct and regulatory risk.

A number of key regulatory projects are underway and
remained a major area of Committee focus. The Committee
received regulatory updates on the Internal Ratings Based (IRB)
programme and maintained oversight of management's delivery
approach, resourcing and prioritisation, monitoring actions to
support ongoing alignment with PRA expectations. The

87

Committee also received regulatory updates on Basel 3.1 and
maintained oversight of management's readiness activities,
including approving the proposed assurance to support
regulatory submissions and implementation readiness. Another
key project is the requirement to apply a Resolvability
Assessment Framework (RAF) and meet the Minimum
Requirement for own funds and Eligible Liabilities (MREL) . The
Committee received quarterly updates on RAF delivery,
including preparations for the Bank's recovery and resolvability
assessments, the associated changes proposed under the
amended DLC Sharing Agreement, and transition planning for
MREL, which commenced on 1 January 2026. The Committee
noted that the key milestones achieved as planned and the
external assurance provided positive feedback on programme
maturity and governance arrangements.

In terms of non-financial risks, the Committee oversaw
continued embedding of the Bank’s Consumer Duty obligations.
Management information has evolved and is frequently
reviewed and challenged by the Committee. Following the
FCA’s review, the Consumer Duty report was given a green
rating, providing external confirmation that the Bank’s approach
was operating as intended. The Committee continued to
monitor good client outcomes, stable complaint trends and
improvements to the Bank’s vulnerable client framework and
customer journey enhancements across Private Client,
Transactional Banking and Investec Save.

Operational resilience remains a key area of focus and the
Committee devoted significant time to cyber security, data
governance and third-party risk. This included oversight of the
Simulated Targeted Attack and Response — Financial Services
(STAR-FS) assessment, and the Committee monitored
management's progress in delivering the remediation plan. The
Committee also reviewed enhancements to privileged-access
management, cloud-provider concentration risk and the
governance of emerging risks, including the responsible use of
Al, with a focus on business enablement, risk management,
people capability and governance.

Fraud risk remains heightened, driven in part by increasing
prevalence of Al-enabled threats, and the Committee monitored
enhancements to fraud-prevention controls and financial crime
tooling in response.

Role of the Committee

The role of the Committee is to review, on behalf of the Board,
the range of risks facing the business. The Committee
performs this function by considering the risk reports
presented and by assessing whether management's actions,
controls and forward-looking plans remain appropriate,
proportionate and effective.

The Committee is an essential part of the Bank’s governance
framework. The Board has delegated the oversight of the
Bank's risk framework to ensure it is appropriate to the size,
scale and nature of the Bank's activities and able to effectively
manage the material risks to which it is exposed. Acting as the
most senior Risk Management Committee of the Bank, the
Committee reviewed and challenged the Bank's risk appetite
and key risk frameworks, including stress tests, and
considered and recommended for approval critical risk
documents, including the ICAAP, ILAAP and CFRP. The
Committee is responsible for ensuring material risks are
identified, monitored and mitigated, and that the resources
allocated to the risk management functions remain adequate
for effectively managing the Bank's risk exposures. The
Committee also provides oversight of the Bank’s compliance
function, including the review of regular reporting from the
Compliance Officer and from the Risk and Controls Forum, and
approval of the annual Compliance Monitoring Programme.

The Committee reports to the Board on how it discharges its
responsibilities and provides appropriate recommendations to
the Board.

Role of the Chair

The role of the Chair of the IBP BRCC includes regular
engagement with senior executives across the Bank and with
the Chair of the DLC BRCC. The Chair meets regularly with risk
functions, Compliance, Head of Finance and Operations and
Head of IT to maintain up-to-date knowledge and stay abreast
of commercial, regulatory and legislative developments, and
challenges facing the business.

Composition and attendance

The Committee is composed solely of independent non-
executive directors, with membership designed to provide the
breadth of risk expertise and commercial acumen it needs to
fulfil its responsibilities. The Chair of the DLC BRCC is a
member of the Committee to ensure interconnection between
the Bank and its parent.

Looking ahead

The Committee will continue to monitor overall levels of risk
within the business as a result of the Bank's accelerated
growth strategy and macro-economic factors.

With the continued uncertainty over the direction of inflation
and interest rates, and the potential of further macro-
economic shocks, the Committee will continue to assess the
impact on clients, credit portfolios, collateral valuations and the
Bank's funding strategy. The Committee will also ensure that
liquidity and capital buffers remain strong and above
regulatory and internal thresholds.

In terms of non-financial risks, fraud, IT, cyber security, data
and third-party risk will continue to be areas of focus. The
Committee will continue to monitor remediation of STAR-FS
actions, assessment of cloud concentration dependencies and
enhancements to Al governance, including the use of Al across
the business, associated risks and controls, accountability
arrangements and overall governance.

Progress continues to be made on embedding the Bank’s ESG
and climate risk approach. This will include ongoing oversight
of the Bank’s Sustainable & Transition Finance Framework,
including progress toward the 2030 targets and the updated
sustainability risk appetite. Monitoring will also include the
FCA’s consultation on motor-finance redress and the
associated data, modelling and operational implications for
the Bank.

The period ahead will be characterised by enhanced oversight
of regulatory projects, including the continued IRB migration,
development of RAF and preparation for phased MREL
transition.

The Committee expects increased supervisory attention in
2026 in areas such as cyber testing, operational resilience,
resolution capabilities and Pillar 2 data and assurance
requirements.

The Committee remains committed to strong, transparent and
forward-looking risk oversight. Through rigorous challenge and
close engagement with management, we have ensured that
the Bank's risk, control and governance frameworks remain
robust, responsive to regulatory expectations and resilient to
an evolving risk environment. This enables Investec to operate
as a cohesive global group while investing responsibly for
long-term growth. The Committee will continue to focus on
emerging risks, operational and cyber resilience, and major
regulatory programmes to support the Bank's ability to operate
safely, serve clients effectively and deliver long-term,
sustainable value.

The Committee continued to review the Bank’s financial risk

that financial risks were being managed within appetite
throughout the period, despite ongoing macro-economic
uncertainty. Financial risk oversight included:

replacement, with ratios remaining above internal and

Going concern statement

In adopting the going concern basis for preparing the
consolidated financial statements, the directors have
considered the Bank’s business activities, objectives and
strategy, principal risks and uncertainties in achieving its
objectives, and performance which are set out in the strategic
report. The directors have performed a robust assessment of
the Bank's financial forecasts across a range of scenarios over
a 12-month period from the date the financial statements are
authorised for issue. Based on the above consideration, the
directors confirm that they have a reasonable expectation that
the Bank has adequate resources to continue in operational
existence for the 12 months from the date the financial
statements are authorised for issue. The directors therefore
consider it appropriate to adopt the going concern basis of
accounting in preparing the accompanying consolidated
financial statements.

Viability statement

The UK Corporate Governance Code requires the Board to
provide both a going concern statement (see page 93) and a
viability statement. The viability statement sets out the Board’s
assessment of Investec Bank plc’s current position, future
prospects, and the principal and emerging risks it faces,
including the period assessed and the rationale for selecting
that timeframe.

The Board has used a three-year assessment period as this is
aligned to the Investec Bank plc’s medium-term capital plans
which incorporate profitability, leverage and capital adequacy
projections and include impact assessments from a number of
stress scenarios. Detailed management information provides
senior management and the Board sufficient and realistic
visibility of Investec Bank plc's viability over the three years to
31 March 2029.

Following confirmation by the IBP BRCC (comprising a majority
of Non-Executive Directors, which includes certain members
of the Audit Committees), the Audit Committee recommended
the viability statement for Board approval.

The Board has identified the principal and emerging risks
facing the Bank and these are highlighted on page 47
onwards, with further detail provided in the Investec pic
(Investec Bank plc's parent company) annual report.

Through its various committees and sub committees, notably
the IBP Audit Committee, the IBP BRCC and the IBP Capital
Committees, the Board regularly carries out a robust
assessment of these principal risks and their potential impact
on the performance, liquidity, solvency, capital and operational
resilience of Investec plc. The activities of these Board sub-
committees and the issues considered by them are described
in the governance section of this report.

The Board considers that prudential risk management is
paramount in all it does. Protection of depositors, customers’
interests, capital adequacy and shareholder returns are key
drivers. The Bank, in keeping with sound governance
practices, has defined roles and responsibilities for the
management of risk and capital in accordance with the three
lines of defence model, i.e. business units, independent risk &
compliance functions and independent internal audit. In
addition, to manage the Bank's risk appetite, there are a
number of detailed statements, frameworks, policies and
governance structures in place. The Board ensures that there
are appropriate resources in place to manage the risks arising
from running the business by having independent Risk and
Capital Management, Compliance, and Financial Control

93

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

functions. These are supplemented by an Internal Audit
function that reports independently to the non-executive Audit
Committee Chair.

The Board believes that the risk and capital management
systems and processes, supported by the conclusions of the
Internal Audit function and the results of their combined
assurance coverage through each assurance function, are
adequate to support Investec Bank plc’s strategy and allow the
Bank to operate within its risk appetite framework.
Performance against the risk appetite framework is reviewed
at each IBP BRCC meeting, with a report-back provided at
each Board meeting.

In terms of the FCA and PRA requirements, Investec Bank plc
is also required to meet regulatory standards with respect to
capital and liquidity. In terms of these requirements, Investec
Bank pic is required to stress its capital and liquidity positions
under a number of severe stress conditions. IBP's stress
testing framework is well embedded in its operations and is
designed to identify and regularly test the Bank’s key
‘vulnerabilities under stress’.

In order to manage liquidity risk, liquidity stress testing is
performed for a range of scenarios, each representing a
different set of assumptions. These include market-wide, firm
specific, and combined scenarios (combination of the market-
wide and firm specific stresses). Investec Bank plc manages its
liquidity risk appetite in relation to combined stress parameters
which represent extreme but plausible circumstances. The
objective is to have sufficient liquidity under a combined stress
scenario to continue to operate for a minimum period as
detailed in the board-approved risk appetite framework. In
addition to these stress scenarios, the Bank’s risk appetite also
requires it to maintain specified minimum levels for both the
liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio and
regulatory minimums of 100% respectively; a minimum cash
and near cash to customer deposit ratio of 25%; and to
maintain low reliance on wholesale funding to fund core asset
growth. Investec ple undertakes an annual Internal Liquidity
Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP) which documents the
approach to liquidity management across the firm. This
document is reviewed and approved by IBP Board Risk and
Capital Committee (IBP BRCC), DLC BRCC and by the IBP, plc
and DLC Boards. Each legal banking entity within Investec
Bank plc is required to be fully self-funded. The Bank currently
has £9.4 billion in cash and near cash assets as at 31 March
2026, representing 41.6% of customer deposits.

Investec Bank plc maintains a three-year capital planning
horizon, developed annually and reviewed semi-annually.
These plans are also updated on an ad-hoc basis in response
to material events. By assessing the capital adequacy under
various economic and internal scenarios, the Bank evaluates
impacts on earnings, asset growth, risk appetite, and liquidity.
Ultimately, this process provides Senior Management and the
Board with the insights necessary to maintain sufficient capital
against internal and regulatory targets over the medium term.
Investec plc targets a CET1 ratio in excess of 10%, a tier 1 ratio
greater than 11%, a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 14% to
17%, and a leverage ratio in excess of 6%.

The parameters used in the capital and liquidity stresses are
reviewed regularly, taking into account the principal and
emerging risks facing the Bank, changes in the business
environments and inputs from business units. Scenarios are
designed considering macro-economic downside risks,
portfolio-specific risk factors and business model
vulnerabilities. Multiple scenarios are considered to account
for the uncertain forward-looking macro-economic
environment.

« Base Case: The UK economy proved to be resilient in the
face of 2025's tariff uncertainty. This performance is
expected to translate into a modest pace of growth in 2026
and beyond, supported by interest rate cuts, increased
investment and a house-building drive. Inflation is expected
to moderate following the mini upswing in 2025, averaging
2.4% in 2026 and returning to target in 2027. Easing price
pressures are anticipated to prompt additional monetary
easing from the Bank of England, with the Bank rate
expected to fall to 3.25% at the end of 2026 and to 3.00% in
2027, Globally economic growth is expected to remain
stable, with annual Global GDP expected to average 3.3%
over the forecast horizon. Advanced market economies are
projected to post modest rates of growth, with the US
expected to outperform with annual rates of growth in
excess of 2%. China is assumed to see GDP growth of
around 4.5% over the medium term. As with the UK, globally
monetary policy is anticipated to return to more neutral
levels.

Investec Bank plc’s expected base case is as approved and
implemented through the budgetary process prior to the onset
of the Middle East conflict and is used for year-end reporting
as well as medium-term business and capital planning
purposes. Notwithstanding this, IBP recognises the heightened
volatility in the external macroeconomic environment and the
resulting uncertainty around certain forecasting assumptions,
including the near-term trajectory of inflation and the
consequent interest rate outlook. These factors have been
considered in forming IBP’s overall assessment of viability.

In assessing stress scenarios for the 2026 capital planning
exercise, two different macroeconomic scenarios were
considered. The first scenario focuses on the risks associated
with Al valuations and private credit and a significant market
shock. The second scenario considers the implications from a

prolonged conflict in Iran and a significant rise in energy prices.

Investec Bank ple implements regulatory scenarios (UK BoE
Bank Capital Stress Scenario) when they are published by the
regulator. At the time of writing the Bank of England had not
published a new regulatory stress test for 2026. Its previous
scenario the 2025 Bank Capital Stress Test (BCST) was
incorporated into the 2025 ICAAP.

The Board has assessed the Bank's viability in its ‘base case’
and stress scenarios. In assessing Investec Bank plc's viability,
a number of assumptions are built into its capital and liquidity
plans. In the stress scenarios these include, for example,
foregoing or reducing dividend payments and asset growth
being curtailed.

Furthermore, an idiosyncratic scenario is run as part of the
capital planning exercise. The idiosyncratic scenario is
triggered by an adverse hypothetical event idiosyncratic to
Investec Bank plc causing elevated losses, negatively setting it
apart from its peers. The scenario narrative assumes such an
event would lead to a negative external signal specific to
Investec, which then triggers further financial and non-
financial consequences.
03 Risk management and CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

governance

DIRECTORS' REPORT
CONTINUED

Investec also carries out ‘reverse stress tests’, i.e., scenarios
that cause the business model to fail. Reverse stress scenarios
are developed thematically, and their impact is assessed in
qualitative and quantitative terms with respect to regulatory
capital and liquidity threshold conditions, taking into account
the loss absorbing effects of the bank's capital stack.
Escalating losses may expose the business model to
unacceptable levels of risk well before regulatory threshold
conditions are breached, and mitigation actions are identified
with the aim to prevent the failure of IBP. Reverse scenarios
are extreme tail events and are considered remote, and mainly
serve the purpose of identifying and addressing potential
weaknesses that may not be identified through the ongoing
risk management and stress testing processes.

In addition, Investec Bank plc performs climate scenario
analysis and risk assessments in line with PRA requirements,
on a proportionate basis for the size and complexity of the
Group. To date, findings indicate that transition and physical
risk is low and IBP has sufficient liquidity and capital to
continue as a going concern and meet regulatory liquidity and
capital requirements.

Investec plc, parent company of Investec Bank plc, is required
to maintain a contingency funding and recovery plan, and a
resolution pack for the Investec plc consolidated Group. The
recovery plan documents how the Board and senior
management will ensure that the Investec plc Group recovers
from extreme financial stress to avoid liquidity and capital
difficulties. The key focus in the recovery plan is the Bank and
the protection of its depositors and other clients.

The BoE confirmed in a letter dated 19 December 2025 the
preferred resolution strategy for Investec plc would remain as
bail-in, with Investec plc and IBP as a material subsidiary,
subject to a binding MREL requirement. The MREL transition
commenced on 1 January 2026 in a phased manner with end
state MREL applying from 1 January 2032. As a bail-in firm,
Investec plc has come into scope of the BoE’s Resolvability
Assessment Framework and will be required to achieve the
three resolvability outcomes by 1 July 2027. Investec plc is
committed to ensuring its resolution capabilities meet the
required regulatory standards.

Investec Bank plc also maintains an operational resilience
framework that defines important business services, impact
tolerances, recovery time objectives and plans to respond
effectively to any disruption. This not only ensures continuity
of business operations but also safequards the interests of key
stakeholders including clients and regulators, as well as
maintaining our reputation, brand and value-creating activities.

95

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

The capital and liquidity plans, stress scenarios, contingency
funding and recovery plans, resolution pack and the risk
appetite statements are reviewed at least annually by the
respective Capital, Risk, and Board Committees. In times of
severe economic distress and if applicable, stress scenarios
are reviewed more regularly; for example, as was the case with
the COVID-19 pandemic and, more recently, during the
escalation of the Middle East conflict. In addition, senior
management hosts an annual risk appetite process at which
the Bank's risk appetite frameworks are reviewed and modified
to take into account risk experience and changes in the
environment. Furthermore, strategic budget processes take
place within each business division at least annually. These
focus on, amongst other things: the business and competitive
landscape; opportunities and challenges including the use of
new and emerging technologies and operational risks relating
to technology, resilience and cyber security; and financial
projections. A summary of these divisional budgets is
presented to the Board during its strategic review process
early in the year.

In assessing the Bank's viability, the Board has taken all of the .
above-mentioned factors, documents and processes into
consideration. The directors can confirm that they have a
reasonable expectation that Investec ple will continue to
operate and meet its liabilities as they fall due over the next
three years.
