IBP Board

The Board plays a crucial role in providing strategic leadership and governance to ensure the Bank's long-term success and integrity.
The Board is responsible for setting and overseeing the implementation of the Bank's strategic direction, ensuring that business
objectives align with the Bank’s mission and values. . !

The Board, comprising both executive and non-executive directors, has the accountability over all material sustainability topics of the
Bank. Updates are presented either verbally or in written format from various IBP Executive Committees and Investec Group Board
committees. The Board met seven times during the year.

Throughout the year, the Board addressed a range of material topics, including low-carbon transition finance — to monitor progress
towards our target of facilitating £14.9 billion of sustainable and transition finance by 2030, which also presents a financial opportunity.
The Board also approved the {BP Tax strategy, fossil fuel policy, environmental policy and climate change statement, and the nature
and biodiversity statement. Furthermore, the Board approved decarbonisation targets for the power generation and oil and gas sectors
in response to climate-related transition risks. In addition, the Board received updates on technology-related risks and opportunities,
including the use of artificial intelligence in business processes, and considered tax governance and client tax-related risks as part of
broader conduct and financial crime reporting. The Board annually reviews the Bank's P&O strategy, presented by the Global Head of
P&O, which covers corporate culture, employee rights, diversity, and employee mental health and wellbeing. Employee remuneration is
managed through the IBP Remuneration Committee, with reports presented to the Board at every meeting and pay gap reports
reviewed annually before publication. Key issues such as data security and privacy risk, cyber security, aspects related to consumer
duty, as well as bribery and corruption related to financial crime, are escalated to the Board through the IBP Board Risk and Capital
Committee (IBP BRCC). Furthermore, At risk controls were discussed with Al-related matters escalated when required through

IBP Board-level committees

IBP Board Risk and Capital Committee (IBP BRCC)
The IBP BRCC is mandated by the Board. This Committee met seven times during the year.

This Committee, comprising non-executive directors, is tasked with reviewing the various risks faced by the Bank, including
sustainability risk. The IBP BRCC fulfits this responsibility by evaluating the risk reports presented to them and assessing whcther the
,actions taken by management are appropriate.

This Committee receives updates from the DLC IT Risk and Governance Committee (DLC ITRGC) and the IBP Executive Risk
Committee (IBP ERC) either in written or verbal format on an ad hoc basis. ‘

During the financial year, the IBP BRCC reviewed several key material topics, including physical climate risks, and climate transition
risks, including regulatory, legal and reputational risks associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy, particularly as they
relate to financed emissions. The Committee also reviewed data privacy and cyber security risks through regular reporting on cyber
resilience, data protection and third-party risk, as well as conduct-related matters, including Consumer Duty and Customer Outcomes
reporting, and financial crime risks through compliance and Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) reporting. Furthermore, the
IBP BRCC reviewed and recommended all sustainability-related policies for approval to the Board. The IRP BRCC approved the
sustainable and transition finance target relating to the IRO of emissions from financing carbon-intensive sectors and reviewed IBP's
exposure to fossil fuel financing.

Material sustainability-related matters are reported to the IBP BRCC on a regular basis and the MLRO reports annually to the IBP BRCC
and to the Board.

IBP Audit Committee

The IBP Audit Committee is mandated by the Board to be the Audit Committee for the Bank. This Committee met five times during the
year. ;
This Committee, comprising non-executive directors, oversees and considers all audit-related matters for the Bank.

During the financial year, the IBP Audit Committee considered sustainability-related matters primarily through its oversight of financial
reporting, internal controls and significant judgements. This included the review of climate-related assumptions and disclosures within
the financial statements, ICAAP processes and macro-economic scenarios, ensuring appropriate governance over climate-related
judgements. The Committee also reviewed matters relating to data protection, cyber risk, operational resilience and third-party risk as
part of its oversight of the control environment. In addition, the Audit Committee reviewed whistleblowing reports and approved the
Whistleblowing Policy, ensuring that appropriate mechanisms are in place for the escalation and investigation of concerns.

The IBP Audit Committee reports material accounting-related sustainability matters to the Board.

DLC Social and Ethics Committee (DLC SEC)

The DLC SEC is mandated by the Investec Group Board. This Committee met four times during the year,

This Committee, comprising both executive and non-executive directors, has accountability for monitoring the Investec Group's
performance in terms of sustainability-related matters. The principal objective of the DLG SFC is tn assist the Investec Group Board in
ensuring that the Investec Group remains a committed, socially responsible corporate citizen in the cantext of the enanamy, snriety,
and environment in which the Investec Group operates.

During the financial year, the Committee monitored the Investec Group's performance across a broad range of sustainahility-related
matters, including climate change, biodiversity, workforce-related topics, client-related risks, and business candunt The Cammittee

“tracked progress against sustainable and transition finance targets and considered developments in climate-related risks and
opportunities, including financed emissions, transition planning and evolving regulatory requirements. The Committee also considered
nature- and biodiversity-related matters, including the financing of nature-related sectors.

In relation to social matters, the Committee received updates on employee wellbeing, diversity and inclusion, and talent development,
including regular reporting from the P&O function. Client-related topics considered included data security and privacy, cyber security,
and access to quality information through Consumer Duty reporting. The Committee also considered the implications of emerging
technologies, including the use of artificial intelligence in business processes and associated risks.

Business conduct remained a key area of focus, with the Committee overseeing matters relating to certain material conduct risk,
whistleblowing, bribery and corruption, financial crime and tax-related governance, The Cammittee alsn cansidered material topics
identified through the DMA, ensuring that these were appropriately reflected in its oversight of sustainability-related risks and impacts.
Material matters are reported to the Board and, where relevant, escalated through the Group's governance structures.

The Committee receives feedback on sustainability matters verbally at every meeting from the Chief Strategy and Sustainability
Officer and on an ad hoc basis from the Global Head of P&O.

The DLC SEC reports material sustainability-related matters to the Board and to the Investec Group Board. Furthermore, material
topics relating to the Bank are escalated by the IBP Chief Risk officer (who is a member of this Committee) to the Board.

The Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer

The Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer is instrumental in steering the Bank's approach to both strategic and sustainability matters
by providing leadership and strategic direction. By embedding sustainability into the core business strategy, this role ensures that
sustainability considerations are integrated into the decision-making processes throughout the Group. This encornpasses identifying
opportunities for sustainable growth, managing risks related to environmental and social factors, and cultivating a culture of
sustainability among our employees. Furthermore, the Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer collaborates with various teams to
design and implement initiatives aligned with our sustainability objectives, such as establishing targets for sustainable and transition
finance and energy sector decarbonisation, and incorporating sustainability into our commercial activities.

As a member of the DLC SEC and Chair of the DLC ESC, the Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer is central to the governance
structure, receiving feedback from the Group sustainability team and the IBP SBF.

The Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer escalates any sustainability-related matters raised by the DLC ESC verbally to the
,DLC SEC.

Supporting function

The Group sustainability team

‘The Group sustainability team is tasked with assessing and reporting on sustainability, escalating relevant matters to the risk teams and
supporting them in identifying sustainahility risks that may impact the Bank and the Investec Group. They also define sectoral policies
to mitigate these risks, ensure compliance with regulatory disclosure requirements, and support business units on sustainability
opportunities relating to products and services. This enables IBP to manage and oversee its sustainability IROs across all businesses
and geographies. Additionally, the Group Sustainability team plays an integral role in monitoring the sustainable and transition finance
targets set for 2030 and guiding the business in setting emission reduction targets.

The Group sustainability team escalates any material sustainability topics to the Chief Strategy and Sustainability Officer.

Management's role in the governance of controls
and procedures to manage and oversee IROs

We are committed to ensuring that our dedicated sustainability
controls and procedures are effectively integrated with other

internal functions. The Bank, in keeping with sound governance

practices, has defined roles and responsibilities for the
management of risk in accordance with the three lines of

defence model, i.e. business line management, an independent

risk function and an independent internal audit function. In
addition, to manage the Bank's risk appetite, there are a
number of detailed statements, frameworks, policies and
governance structures in place.

Overall, the Board ensures that there are appropriate resources

in place to manage the risks arising from running the business
by having independent risk management, compliance and
financial control functions. These are supplemented by an
Internal Audit function that reports independently to the non-
executive Audit Committee Chair.

Controls and procedures relating to sustainability are integrated

across our three lines of defence model.
Business line management:

« Revenue writing business functions: Continued collaboration
exists between the Group sustainability team and the
revenue writing business units. This collaboration is
facilitated through cross-departmental committees and joint
initiatives, like the IBP SBF, that promote the sharing of
insights and best practices. In particular, this forum focuses
on commercial activities within E1 — Climate change in
relation to the positive impacts of low-carbon transition
finance and the financial opportunities for sustainable and
transition finance, through setting and monitoring our
progress towards our sustainable and transition finance
target. Sustainability controls and procedures related to
transition finance, including the establishment of our
sustainable and transition finance targets, are managed by
the management teams within each revenue-generating
business

* People & Organisation (P&O): Our P&O team takes
accountability for actioning and monitoring our material IROs
within S1—- Our people, which includes employee wellbeing,
and recruitment and development of diverse talent. The
Board has delegated the responsibility of monitoring Board
diversity targets to the IBP Nomination Committee, which

reviews the composition of the Board at each of its meetings.
Progress on diversity targets is escalated to the Board by the

P&O team. Assessments of employee wellbeing, recruitment

and development of diverse talent are escalated to the Board

as and when required

Marketing: The marketing function is responsible for the
material matters identified in $4 — Our clients, pertaining to
client engagement and marketing. This responsibility
encompasses the processes and controls established for
external client communications related to sustainability
claims, with oversight provided by the Group sustainability
team, the legal team and the compliance team

Governance of target-setting

The Board, DLC SEC and DLC ESC, along with senior executive
management, are accountable for monitoring the progress
against establishing sustainability-related targets for material
IROs.

Approval for these targets is granted by the Board and the DLC
SEC while the DLC ESC ensures alignment with the overall
Investec Group sustainability strategy.

Sustainability-related skills of the Board and
Executives

The DLC SEC supports the Board through detailed oversight of
sustainability-related matters, including climate, social impact,
ethics, governance and stakeholder-related considerations,
while the Board retains ultimate accountability for sustainability
governance across the Group.

A fundamental aspect of governance is ensuring the
effectiveness of the Board in fulfilling its responsibilities. The
composition of the Board has been designed to ensure the
appropriate mix of knowledge, skills, experience, independence
and diversity. Consideration is given towards the collective
skills, knowledge and experience of the directors when
assessing the overall composition and suitability of the Board.
In addition to a range of skills, the Board also values the innate
differences in approach and thinking styles that result from the
varied backgrounds and experiences of our directors.

Recognising any gaps, the Board seeks to invest in continuous
professional development by providing targeted development
programmes, workshops and access to expert consultations to
enhance the sustainability knowledge of all directors through
the directors’ development plan. Regular performance reviews
are conducted to monitor progress, ensuring that the Board
remains well equipped to address emerging sustainability
challenges.

The Board leverages the robust in-house expertise of teams
managing key sustainability matters alongside its members’
specialised knowledge. These in-house teams bring deep
expertise in areas such as environmental management, social

responsibility, renewable energy and corporate governance,
providing comprehensive insights into sustainability matters.
For complex or emerging challenges, the Board accesses
external experts, ensuring a blend of internal strengths and
external resources. Additionally, the Board fosters continuous
enhancement of expertise within the Bank through
collaboration, professional development and employee
engagement mechanisms.

These initiatives are designed to build the Board's Capacity to
effectively understand and oversee the Bank’s material
sustainability matters.

Consideration of IRQs in relation to strategy and
business activities

All material IROs have already been effectively integrated into

- the relevant business and operational functions within the

Bank. Importantly, these material IROs do not change our
current strategy or business activities, as we have consistently
adopted an integrated approach to sustainability for many
years. We incorporate sustainability considerations into our
daily operations and decision-making processes to support a
sustainable, long-term vision. Our commitment to sustainability
is deeply ingrained in our operations and business practices,
enabling us to manage these IROs effectively without requiring
adjustments to our established strategic direction.

Integration of sustainability-related performance
into incentive schemes

As part of IBP’s approach to sustainability governance,
Executive Directors and senior management are subject to
sustainability-related performance objectives linked to diversity
and inclusion. These objectives include progress against the
Women in Finance Charter target of achieving at least 35%
female representation in senior leadership positions by 2027.
Performance against this sustainability-related target is
considered as part of the assessment of variable remuneration.
We intend to further develop our remuneration framework for
IBP Executives through the incorporation of additional
sustainability-related performance measures over time.

Our sustainability strategy is intrinsically linked to our overarching purpose of creating enduring worth for all stakeholders. By
integrating sustainability into our core business practices, we aim to deliver long-term value that transcends financial performance,
fostering resilience in both our operations and the clients we serve. Our commitment to sustainable finance not only supports our
clients in their transitions to greener practices but also aligns with our goal of promoting economic, social and environmental
wellbeing. We aim to enhance our ability to generate lasting impact, ensuring that our business contributes positively to society
while securing a sustainable future for generations to come. Our business model, and operational and strategic overview are
disclosed on page 10 of this report. Our sustainability strategy applies to all geographies and business activities within IBP.

Central to our purpose to create enduring worth is the belief that sustainability is integral to our business. Our commercial
strategies work with a broad stakeholder perspective from inception and we are conscious about the impact they make in the
world. Our focus areas are addressing climate change and supporting socioeconomic progress which are fundamental to our

sustainability strategy.

These focus areas are supported by our alignment to the Sustainable Development Goals, reflecting how we allocate capital and
support sustainable economic development across our core markets.

We have market-leading, distinctive client franchises. The Investec distinction is embodied in our entrepreneurial culture, supported

environment. Ours is a culture that values purposeful thinking and stimulates extraordinary performance. We take pride in the

Products and services relating to our material IROs

IBP offers a comprehensive range of products and services
tailored to distinct customer groups across significant markets.
For our sustainability-focused activities we are guided by our
Sustainable and Transition Finance Classification Framework,
which supports both environmentally and socially sustainable
commercial initiatives.

Our sustainability-focused products and services reflect our
ambition to achieving our sustainability-related goals,
particularly our target to facilitate £14.9 billion for IBP in
sustainable and transition finance by 2030. In the first year of
measuring progress towards our target, we are pleased to have
achieved £2.6 billion in sustainable and transition finance.

Private Client Banking activities: Our Private Client Banking
division provides high-touch and high-tech solutions such as
transactional banking, lending, private capital, savings and
foreign exchange services specifically designed for high net
worth (HNW) private clients. These offerings cater to active
wealth creators with annual incomes typically exceeding
£300,000 and net asset values above £3 million, primarily
serving clients in the UK and the Channet Islands.

Sustainability-related products for this group primarily involve
mortgage lending, focusing on financing higher Energy
Performance Certificate (EPC)-rated properties. This lending
supports our efforts in energy transition finance and in
addressing financed emissions, specifically targeting E1 -
Climate change.

Corporate and Investment Banking activities: In our
Corporate and Investment Banking activities, we deliver client-
centric and solution-driven services, including lending, treasury
and risk management solutions, advisory and institutional
research, as well as sales and trading. This division serves a
broad spectrum of clients, including corporate, private,
intermediary, government, and institutional entities across the
UK, Europe, Channel Islands, the USA, and India.

Typically, sustainability-related offerings are lending products,
including sustainability-linked loans, where key loan terms,
including adjustments in the interest rate, are tied to the
borrower's achievement of specific sustainability targets. This
structure incentivises companies to enhance their sustainability
performance. Additionally, lending can be classified as
sustainable finance based on the company’s profile if 90% of its
revenues are derived from sustainable activities or if the
proceeds are specifically allocated to sustainable
environmental or social initiatives (as recommended by the EU
Sustainable Finance Disclosure Recommendations). These
products focus on addressing E1 — Climate change.

Sustainability-related products and services for our Corporate
and Investment Banking clients include:

« Lending to properties: Within our real estate business, we

provide loans to properties with A and B graded EPC ratings
to promote energy efficiency. For properties with lower EPC
ratings, we look to finance energy-efficiency upgrades that

improve the EPC ratings to Aor 8

Supporting renewable projects: In our Energy and
Infrastructure business, we support projects that utilise
renewable sources such as wind, solar, battery storage,
renewable natural gas and EV infrastructure, along with
digital infrastructure initiatives

« Sustainable funding solutions: Through our Direct Lending

socially sustainable activities that have defined social

Financing environmentally sustainable solutions: In our asset

EVs, renewable energy generation, energy-efficiency

Managing fossil fuel exposures: We manage our fossil fuel

Additionally, in pursuit of influencing our clients and suppliers to

Resilience of our strategy and business model

IBP evaluates the resilience of our strategy and business model
in terms of its ability to identify material impacts, address
associated risks and capitalise on resulting opportunities.

This resilience is supported through the IBP BRCC from which

During the financial year ending 31 March 2026, Investec conducted a DMA, supported by an external adviser, to identify
sustainability-related {ROs material to the Group and its stakeholders.

The assessment was performed in accordance with ESRS 1 and ESRS 2 requirements, applying the principle of double materiality
by considering both impact materiality, relating to the Group's impacts on society and the environment, and financial materiality,
relating to how sustainability matters may affect financial performance through risks and opportunities,

The DMA covered IBP’s upstream, own operations and downstream value chain activities across short-, medium- and long-term
time horizons (as defined in the basis of preparation)

Methodology and approach

The DMA followed a structured four-step process comprising Frame, Identify, Assess and Complete as shown in the diagram
below. ;

Key enhancements in 2026

The DMA methodology was refined compared to the prior financial year to strengthen alignment with internal risk management
frameworks, enhance value chain analysis and improve the robustness of the scoring approach.

Further enhancements included more structured integration of stakeholder inputs into both the identification and scoring of IROs
and improved identification of emerging sustainability topics. IBP will continue to review IROs annually and perform a
comprehensive DMA every two years. Where significant changes in the business, operating environment, regulatory landscape or
stakeholder expectations are identified, IBP will assess whether these changes may result in new or materially different IROs. In
such cases, a targeted reassessment will be performed, including updates to the materiality assessment and, where required,
disclosures and governance processes will be adapted accordingly.

1. Frame and sector research, and are considered across short-,

The framing stage established the context for the assessment
by analysing IBP’s operating environment, business model,
strategy and value chain. This included mapping activities
across the value chain, identifying key stakeholder groups and
considering external drivers such as regulatory developments
and industry trends.

This process defined the scope of the DMA, including value
chain boundaries, relevant time horizons and key stakeholders.

2. Identify

Building on the framing stage, IBP identified a comprehensive
universe of sustainability topics and associated IROs across the
value chain. Topics were identified through horizon scanning,
drawing on internal strategy, peer analysis, international
frameworks (including Global Reporting Initiative (GR),
Sustainability Accounting Standard Board (SASB), Principles for
Responsible Banking (PRB) and the UN United Nations
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), regulatory
developments and sector research.

Stakeholder input was obtained through internal workshops
and was used to inform both the identification and scoring of
IROs.

A longlist of IROs were identified through a combination of
value chain analysis, stakeholder mapping and external context
analysis. A downstream hotspot analysis, aligned with the
United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative
(UNEP Fl) Impact Protocol for Banks, was applied to identify
areas of elevated impact risk based on sectoral and geographic
exposure, within Investec's downstream value chain. Impacts
were classified as positive or negative, and IROs were identified
using an integrated approach to ensure that impacts and
related financial risks and opportunities were considered
together. This resulted in a comprehensive universe of
sustainability topics and a longlist of IROs across
environmental, social, governance and entity-specific themes.

As part of this identification process, IBP specifically considers
climate-related transition events across its value chain,
including changes in climate policy and regulation (such as
carbon pricing), technological developments, shifts in market
demand and customer behaviour, and evolving stakeholder
expectations. These transition drivers are identified through
horizon scanning, regulatory analysis, stakeholder engagement

medium-~ and long-term time horizons, Where relevant, climate-
related scenario analysis is used to support the identification of
potential transition pathways and associated risks and
opportunities.

3. Assess

Identified IROs, including both positive and negative impacts,
were assessed and prioritised based on impact and financial
materiality, using internal data and external research.

Impact materiality was assessed based on severity, considering
scale, scope and irremediability (for negative impacts), together
with likelihood assessed for potential impact. In line with ESRS
requirements, severe negative human rights impacts may be
considered material where severity takes precedence over
likelihood. Financial materiality was assessed based on the
potential magnitude and likelihood of financial effects across
relevant risk categories, including credit, market, operational,
reputational and regulatory risks. Financial materiality was
assessed based on the potential magnitude and likelihood of
financial effects. in line with ESRS 1 requirements, risks with low
probability but high potential financial impact were specifically
considered as part of the assessment, including through expert
judgement and the application of materiality thresholds.

Assessments were conducted across short-, medium- and
long-term time horizons, reflecting how potential impacts, risks
and opportunities may evolve over time. A standardised scoring
methodology, based on predefined criteria and aligned with
internal risk management frameworks, was applied to prioritise
IROs, supported by expert judgement through workshops and
subject matter expert input.

Materiality thresholds, aligned with the Group’s risk framework,
were applied to consolidate results into a materiality matrix and
identify potentially material IROs for validation.

The identified climate-related physical hazards and transition
events are assessed to determine the extent to which IBP’s
assets and business activities may be exposed including
consideration of likelihood, magnitude and duration of potential
financial effects.

to multi-layered validation, including subject matter expert
review, cross-functional workshops and external adviser
challenge. Final outcomes were reviewed and approved
through established governance processes, including executive
management, the DLC SEC and the Board.

Integration of sustainability-related risks into risk management processes

Sustainability risk is identified as a principal risk within IBP and is managed in accordance with IBP’s general risk management
approach (refer to page 49). This risk is defined as the risk that our lending and investing activities give rise to unintended climate,
environmental, social and economic consequences. We regard sustainability risk as equally significant as principal risks, including
credit, operational and market risks. By assessing sustainability risks alongside other risk categories within the enterprise risk
management framework, we can identify potential financial and reputational impacts on our business.

The outcomes of our DMA align closely with existing material risks managed by the Group, indicating that sustainability-related
risks and opportunities are integrated into decision-making, risk governance and business activities.

Reporting on material IROs

Following the DMA, IBP mapped its material IROs to the ESRS mandatory disclosure requirements and data points within the topical
standards where relevant. Tne material IROs map to the following topics, which forms the basis of preparation for this sustainability
statement: E1 ~ Climate change, E4 ~ Biodiversity and ecosystems, $1~ Our people, $4 ~ Our clients, G1 - Business conduct and
entity-specific topics which include financial crime, Client tax practices and due diligence, cyber security and artificial intelligence.

Non-material topics

The following topics were not deemed material: E2 - Pollution, E3 - Water and marine resources, E5 - Resource use and circular
economy, $2 - Workers in the value chain and $3 - Affected communities. These topics did not cross our materiality threshold and
are therefore omitted from the corresponding disclosure requirements. Additionally, our business model is centred on banking and
wealth management, rather than on sectors such as industrial, manufacturing or extraction, where direct pollution risks, circular
economy impacts and impacts on workers in the value chain are more pronounced. They will be reassessed for relevance during
our next DMA.

Summary of material IROs

The outcome from our DMA highlighted 20 material IROs as
identified by our stakeholders. Material IROs are predominantly
concentrated in our own operations and downstream value
chain, reflecting the significance of IBP’s financing activities.

From an environmental perspective, climate change (ESRS E1)}
was identified as a key material topic, with material IROs
relating to financed emissions, physical climate risks and
transition risks arising from regulatory, market and
technological changes. In addition, an opportunity was
identified in relation to sustainable and transition finance,
reflecting IBP’s role in supporting the transition to a low-carbon
economy. Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4) was also
identified as material, with impacts linked to the financing of
sectors with potential biodiversity impact in the downstream
value chain.

From a social perspective, material IROs relate to IBP’s
employees (ESRS Si), including employee wellbeing and Board
diversity. These reflect both positive impacts and associated
financial risks linked to the attraction, retention and
development of employees.

Investec Bank ple Annual Financial Statements 2026

Material IROs were also identified in relation to clients (ESRS
$4), particularly regarding data security and privacy, access to
information and cyber security. These IROs reflect the
increasing importance of digital capabilities and responsible
technology use in delivering client outcomes.

From a governance perspective (ESRS G1), material IROs
relate to business conduct, including conduct risk,
whistleblowing, bribery and corruption, financial crime, and
client tax practices and due diligence. in addition, entity-
specific IROs relating to artificial intelligence were identified,
including both risks associated with misuse and opportunities
linked to process optimisation. These represent key areas of
financial and reputational risk and are critical to maintaining
stakeholder trust and regulatory compliance.

Overall, the identified IROs suggest that IBP’s most material
sustainability impacts and financial risks and opportunities are
closely linked to its core banking activities, particularly within its
lending and investment portfolio.

Climate change

Transition plan for climate change
mitigation

The Group has commenced the development of its transition
plan, building on our existing climate-related strategy and
commitments through a phased approach. As part of this, we
have initiated Phase | of our transition plan, which establishes
initial decarbonisation targets and supports the ongoing
development of a comprehensive plan over time. This
represents an initial phase and does not yet constitute a fully
developed transition plan as defined under emerging regulatory
expectations.

Our transition plan is aligned with our ambition to achieve net
zero by 2050 and draws on the guidance set out by the
Transition Plan Taskforce as endorsed by the International
Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). In developing our
approach, we consider the complexities of our business in the
context of climate change, as well as the interlinkages between
climate change and nature-related impacts, including
ecosystem resilience. In establishing our transition plan, we
continue to use three channels of impact as our foundation:

1. Meeting our fossil fuel exposure commitments: aligned to the
double materiality matter identified ~ climate change
mitigation (fossil fuel financing)

2. Driving sustainable and transition finance activities: aligned
to the double materiality matter identified ~ climate change
mitigation (energy transition finance)

3. Influencing and advocating for our clients and suppliers to
effectively pursue decarbonisation: aligned to the material
IRO identified ~ climate change mitigation (financed
emissions}. As part of our transition plan, this includes an
engagement-led approach to support improved emissions
transparency, transition planning and alignment with our
sustainability objectives.

IGP is currently developing a transition plan around our existing
climate-related strategy and commitments, which we expect to
adopt in the next two years.

Material IROs relating to climate change

We acknowledge that climate change is material and poses
significant risks and opportunities, including its ability to
generate value for stakeholders over time. We recognise and
support the aims of the Paris Agreement goals and are
committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050", taking
into account the complexities of the business in relation to
climate change. Additionally, we acknowledge the clear link
between climate change and ecosystem loss, and our impact
through our activities on healthy and resilient ecosystems.

The process for identifying and assessing material impacts,
risks and opportunities is described on page 303 and applies to
this topic.

The main challenges we face include navigating the
complexities of climate risks, adapting to regulatory changes,
and balancing economic growth with sustainability objectives.
We are committed to continue enhancing our climate risk
management and sustainability data capabilities, ensuring
transparency in our sustainability reporting and alignment with
evolving regulatory frameworks.

Emissions from IBP’s own operations (Scope 1 and Scope 2), as
well as all Scope 3 all categories excluding Scope 3: Category
15 - financed emissions, represent a negligible portion of the
total emissions within IBP's value chain. All Scope 3 categories
excluding Category 15 account for less than 1% of total Scope 3
emissions. Accordingly, Scopel, Scope 2 and all other Scope 3
emissions have been classified as immaterial and are therefore
not included in this Sustainability Statement. However, IBP
continues to work on reducing operational emissions and
unavoidable residual emissions are offset through the purchase
of carbon credits from verified, high quality and ethical carbon
removal projects. Further information on our operational
emissions can be found in our 2026 Integrated Sustainability
Report on our website.

During the DMA, climate-related IROs were assessed across
IBP’s lending and investment activities, incorporating both
transition and physical climate considerations.

The assessment identified material climate-related IROs
primarily linked to climate change mitigation, as well as financial
risks arising from physical climate hazards. These include
positive and negative impacts associated with financing
activities, alongside financial risks and opportunities driven by
the transition to a low-carbon economy.

From a financial perspective, IBP is exposed to transition risks
driven by evolving regulation, carbon pricing, technolagical
change, and shifting consumer preferences, which may affect
asset values, revenues, and credit risk, particularly across
carbon-intensive sectors. In addition, physical risks, including
acute and chronic hazards such as flooding, may impact
borrower asset values, operations, and supply chains over
short-, medium-, and long-term time horizons.

At the same time, opportunities arise through the expansion of
sustainable and transition finance activities, supporting client
decarbonisation while enabling participation in emerging low-
carbon markets.

These IRQs primarily materialise through IBP’s banking activities
and represent the key channels through which climate-related
factors affect the Group's business model and strategy. Further
detail on these IRQs is provided in the table below.

3 Net zero commitment by 2050: A pledge to reduce GHG emissions across all Scopes (1, 2 and 3) to as close to zero as possible by 2050, with any remaining emissions
balanced by removing an equivalent amount from the atmosphere. This commitment aligns with the goals of the Paris Agreement to limit global warming to well below

2°C, and preferably to 1.5°C, above pre-industrial levels.

Positive impact associated with low carbon transition
finance

We recognise the significant positive impact that sustainable
and transition finance can have in supporting the transition toa
low-carbon economy. By providing financial support for
renewable energy projects and initiatives aimed at reducing
carbon emissions, we support client decarbonisation and
contribute to reducing financed emissions over time. This not
only helps to mitigate the adverse effects of traditional energy
sources but also support the development of resilient and
sustainable infrastructure, promotes economic growth, and
contributes to broader social and environmental outcomes.

Negative impact associated with financing carbon-intensive
sectors

Financing carbon-intensive sectors contributes to financed
emissions and associated climate-related impacts across our
lending and investment portfolios. These impacts arise primarily
downstream through client activities and may result in
continued GHG emissions where transition pathways are not
yet fully realised.

Financial opportunity associated with sustainable and
transition finance

Our stakeholders identified sustainable and transition finance
lending as a financial opportunity from new markets and
products, resulting in positive revenues and financial
performance. Expanding our sustainable and transition finance
offering enables us to support client decarbonisation while
accessing new markets and revenue streams. In pursuit of our
purpose to create enduring worth, and as part of our

313

commitment to reaching net zero by 2050, we have committed
to mobilise £14.9 billion by 2030. This represents a key lever in
delivering our sustainability strategy and supporting long-term
value creation.

Financial risk associated with physical climate risk

Physical climate risks arise from acute and chronic climate
hazards, including flooding, extreme weather events and long-
term shifts in climate patterns. These risks may impact
borrower operations, asset values and supply chains,
potentially resulting in reduced collateral values, business
disruption and increased credit risk across our lending portfolio.

IBP currently assesses physical climate risk in selected
portfolios, including real estate and power generation annually,
supplemented by occasional stress testing in line with Bank of
England expectations. These assessments support our
understanding of portfolio exposure to physical climate risks
over relevant time horizons and help inform our risk
management approach.

Further detail on our assessment of physical climate risks and
the resilience of our strategy and business model is provided in
the resilience section of this report.

Financial risk associated with climate transition risks

We are continuously exploring ways to reduce our Scope 3
financed emissions, category 15: Investments and remain
committed to advocating for climate action. Climate transition
risks arise from evolving regulation, carbon pricing, technology
change and shifting consumer preferences across carbon-

06 Sustainability statement

SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT
CONTINUED

intensive sectors, which may adversely impact asset values,
revenues and creditworthiness of counterparties.

Our approach is collaborative, balancing our ambitions with
regional regulations and transition plans. It is important to
understand that reductions may not occur annually; rather,
they will take place over time as our business evolves and as
the countries and sectors implement their respective net-zero
strategies. Furthermore, we are committed to managing our
fossil fuel financing and have already achieved our goal of zero
coal exposure in our loan portfolio as of September 2024, well
ahead of the original target date of 31 March 2027. Additionally,
we manage our oil and gas exposures, with all transactions in
this sector undergoing thorough screening by the Group
sustainability team. If any concerns arise, the transaction is
presented to the IBP ERC, which will decide whether to
proceed, taking into account the context of the values and
guardrails established within the Bank. These risks are closely
linked to financed emissions and are expected to materialise
over short-, medium- and long-term time horizons. In response,
we actively manage exposures to high-carbon sectors through

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

sector-specific targets, client engagement and internal
governance processes, ensuring alignment with our risk
appetite and sustainability strategy.

Financial risk associated with climate transition risks - Legal,
reputational, technology and market demand

Climate transition risks may arise from evolving regulatory
expectations, technological developments, shifting market
demand, and increasing scrutiny of sustainability-related
disclosures. These risks include potential legal and compliance
exposure, increased operational costs, and reputational
damage, particularly in relation to greenwashing, where
sustainability-related claims may be perceived as misleading,
unsubstantiated or inconsistent.

These risks primarily materialise across IBP’s value chain
through client-facing activities, product development, and
public disclosures, and may impact stakeholder trust, brand
value, and the Bank's ability to access sustainable finance
opportunities over the short-, medium- and long-term.

Climate transition risks:

Policy: Environmental policy and climate change statement

The policy underscores our role in funding a sustainable
economy and promoting carbon reduction as central to our
climate change strategy. It states that we aim to reduce Scope
3 financed emissions, category 15: Investments by leveraging
IBP’s expertise in advisory, lending and investing to support
clients' transition to a low-carbon economy. The policy commits
us to financing innovative solutions that accelerate
decarbonisation, actively measuring and accounting for carbon
emissions through participation in initiatives like PCAF.
Furthermore, the policy outlines that environmental
considerations are integrated into all lending and investment
decisions. Additionally, we adopt a cautious and orderly
approach to transitioning sectors critical to the economy, such
as energy, balancing financial, socio-economic and
environmental factors.

« Scope of the policy: The policy covers the Investec Group
which includes IBP. In addition to our own carbon footprint it
focus on measuring and reducing emissions in our value

chain relating to lending and investing activities

Accountability: For the Bank, accountability for the
implementation lies with the Board. Any future targets set as
part of our transition plan will be approved by IBP ERC, DLC
SEC and the Board. The Board will be accountable for
progress against these targets

Publication status: This is a public policy last updated in
March 2026 with a review cycle of every two years. This
policy is on our website here.

Tracking the effectiveness of our policy

IBP tracks the effectiveness of its efforts to reduce Scope 3
financed emissions, category 15: Investments through regular
progress updates to the DLC ESC. Our reported Scope 3
financed emissions, category 15: Investments undergo a
rigorous verification and approval process involving individual
business units the IBP Chief Risk Officer. The emissions data is
then presented to the DLC ESC and DLC SEC through the
annual reporting sign-off process for oversight. Additionally, we
have commenced Phase | of our decarbonisation plan, adopting
a bottom-up approach that incorporates input and ownership
from relevant business units through the IBP SBF framework.
We will track and report our progress towards emissions
reduction targets to the Board, the IBP BRCC, the DLC ESC and
the DLC SEC, ensuring continuous oversight of delivery against
our transition objectives.

Policy: Fossil fuel policy

The fossil fuel policy outlines the Investec Group's approach to
fossil fuels across its lending, investing and advisory activities.
Driven by a commitment to sustainability and the urgency of
climate change, the policy details restrictions and conditions for
financing coal, oil and gas projects. It also describes the
Investec Group's commitment to net zero by 2050, its adoption
of screening for high-risk transactions, support for a just energy
transition, and our approach to transparency and reporting on
our fossil fuel exposure.

» Scope of the policy: The policy encompasses the entire
Investec Group, including IBP, and pertains to our clients
throughout the value chain, specifically focusing on our
lending, investing and advisory activities

« Accountability: For the Bank, accountability for the
implementation lies with the Board. Targets are approved by
the Board, IBP ERC and IBP BRCC

Publication status: This is a public policy last updated in

policy is on our website here.

Tracking the effectiveness of our policy

IBP tracks the effectiveness of its performance against the
fossil fuel policy through continuous monitoring and
management of existing oil and gas exposures, with a focus on
minimising these exposures wherever possible in line with our
fossil fuel policy commitments. To ensure implementation of
this policy, the Group sustainability team performs screening on
every oil and gas transaction. Where a transaction is not
aligned with our fossil fuel policy, it will get escalated to the IBP
ERC. Furthermore, all fossil fuel-related exposures are reported
bi-annually to the Board, DLC ESC, DLC BRCC, and the DLC
SEC and at each IBP BRCC meeting. This allows us to assess
our progress against our commitments and enables
adjustments and strategic decisions to align with our
sustainability goals. These communication channels ensure that
our fossil fuel policy remains effective, adapts to emerging risks
and aligns with our overarching commitment to gradually
reduce fossil fuel exposure over time while taking into account
any geopolitical or economic challenges.

Framework: Sustainable and Transition Finance
Classification Framework

Our approach to sustainable finance is underpinned by our
commitment to driving positive environmental and social
outcomes while ensuring long-term financial resilience. In
developing our Sustainable and Transition Finance
Classification Framework, we considered a range of
internationally recognised frameworks and market quidance to
support alignment with global sustainability objectives.

This framework provides the environmental and social
sustainable and transition finance classification criteria for
sustainable and transition finance for the Investec Group.

The framework utilises a traffic light system to classify
environmentally sustainable finance activities (green),
transition finance activities (amber) and activities that do

not qualify as sustainable nor transition finance (red). Social
sustainable finance activities are not classified by a traffic light
system, but consider defined target populations and social
outcomes. The purpose of this framework is to guide the
Investec Group's lending activities in supporting a more
sustainable future and the transition to a low-carbon economy
while also addressing social sustainability.

* Scope of the framework: The framework encompasses
the entire Investec Group, including IBP, but excludes the
Investec Wealth & Investment business. it specifically
pertains to our clients within the value chain, focusing

primarily on our lending activities

Accountability: For the Bank, accountability for the
implementation lies with the Board. Targets were approved
by the Board, IBP ERC and IBP 8RCC, DLC ESC and the DLC
SEC

Publication status: This is a public framework which was last
updated in May 2026, with a review cycle of two years.
This framework is on our website here.

Tracking the effectiveness of the framework

IBP tracks the effectiveness of the Investec Group's
Sustainable and Transition Finance Classification Framework
through progress updated to the Board, the DLC ESC and the
DLC SEC twice a year.

Furthermore the IBP SBF, which is mandated by the IBP
Executives plays a pivotal role in promoting knowledge sharing
and fostering collaboration across the Bank. This forum meets
fortnightly and are composed of business unit representatives,
management and Executives. By regularly identifying and
evaluating sustainability-related commercial opportunities, the
forum aims to assist the Group sustainability team in ensuring
that the Sustainable and Transition Finance Classification
Framework remains dynamic and responsive to emerging
trends and challenges. Additionally, the Sustainable Business
Forum coordinates key sustainability projects, including the
monitoring of progress towards the sustainable and transition
finance target, which serves as a measurable indicator of the
Framework’s impact.

The effectiveness of the Sustainable and Transition Finance
Classification Framework is further monitored through reporting
mechanisms, whereby the chair of the IBP SBF communicates
significant sustainability-related matters to the DLC ESC and,
when relevant, to the OLC SEC, IBP ERC, IBP BRCC and the
Board. This continuous feedback loop allows IBP to assess
progress against the sustainable and transition finance target,
make informed adjustments and ensure alignment with the
Bank's strategic goals, thereby maintaining the Framework’s
relevance and effectiveness in driving sustainable growth.

Resilience of our strategy and business
model! in relation to climate change

The Bank of England’s 2021 Climate Biennial Exploratory
Scenario (CBES) continues to inform the framework for our
climate scenario analysis. While the Bank of England did not
conduct a new CBES exercise during the FY2026 reporting
period, as these assessments are performed periodically rather
than annually, the principles established in its most recent
assessment (published in 2022) remain relevant. These
scenarios are designed to evaluate the resilience of banks to a
range of adverse economic conditions, particularly those arising
from climate-related and broader systemic risks, and to assess
how institutions can withstand shocks such as economic
downturns, market volatility and significant shifts in climate-
related factors.

Such stress testing approaches are important for identifying
vulnerabilities within the financial system and ensuring that
banks maintain sufficient capital buffers and effective risk
management practices to mitigate potential losses.

In Supervisory Statement $S3/19, the Prudential Regulation
Authority (PRA) outlines its expectations for firms to assess
climate-related financial risks over both short- and long-term
time horizons. Climate scenario analysis continues to be
performed at the Investec pic level, which encompasses IBP as
a subsidiary, ensuring appropriate coverage within Group-level
assessments.

In addition, the PRA’s updated expectations under Supervisory
Statement SS5/25 are being addressed through cross-
functional working groups within IBP, spanning all risk
disciplines. In line with SS5/25, IBP is undertaking an internal
review of its current approach to managing climate-related
risks, to be completed by June 2026. This review will identify
any gaps relative to PRA expectations and inform the
development of a plan to address these gaps over an
appropriate timeframe.

During 2024, Investec plc carried out its climate risk
assessment which was broadly a repeat of the 2022 climate
risk assessment. For each of the assessed sectors (property,
transportation, energy and manufacturing), a transition
narrative was developed. This narrative focused on key
technological and policy/ legislation measures necessary to
achieve decarbonisation, specific to each sector. Due to the
high uncertainty of both technological readiness and the
duration of the policy/legislation process (including
jurisdictional misalignment of scope and timing), no specific
timeframe was specified in these narratives. The aim was to
focus on understanding the impact of the sector-specific
transition narrative on top 100 assets within IBP’s portfolio, and
through this process assess whether there are any high risk-
assets in the portfolio. In addition, a flood risk assessment on
HNW mortgages within Investec plc’s top 100 assets was
performed. This risk assessment can therefore not be tied to
any specific time frame, though it is noted that in reality
sectoral time frames for full decarbonisation can range from
several years to multiple decades. This approach is
proportionate to the scale and complexity of the firm, in line
with SS3/19.

Sectors were all assessed for transition risk and HNW
mortgages were assessed for physical risk. Moreover, the
exposures in the asset level review were also assessed against
the ‘traffic light system’ in the Group’s Sustainable and
Transition Finance Classification Framework.

Property sector

The property sector faces climate transition and physical risks,
with flooding emerging as a primary concern in the UK.
Decarbonising this sector requires substantial improvements in
insulation and the electrification of space and water heating,
which can impose considerable costs on property owners and
landlords, especially as they navigate tighter regulations
recently reintroduced by the UK Labour Government.
Enhancing the energy efficiency of buildings in the UK through
measures such as improved insulation and the transition to
electric heating systems, is critical. Furthermore, stricter rules
regarding energy efficiency will be implemented for rental
properties, aimed at reducing carbon emissions across the
sector.

Transition risk event - mandates on and regulation of existing
products and services: The implications of the evolving EPC
requirements present a key risk, as all residential tenancies for
private landiords will need to achieve a minimum EPC rating of
C by 2030, while commercial tenancies must meet this
standard by April 2027, escalating to B by the same year.
Additionally, the ban on gas boilers in new buildings after 2025
will lead to further transition costs for property owners.
However, IBP has identified mitigants to address these
challenges. Exemptions to the minimum EPC requirements exist
for listed buildings or older properties with capped EPC ratings,
and notably, more than 90% of HNW mortgages have valid EPC
ratings, complying with existing regulations. IBP also provides
lending facilities specifically for energy-efficiency improvement
works, ensuring that all new lending adheres to minimum EPC
and Building Research Establishment Environmental
Assessment Methodology (BREEAM) standards, which
enhances the quality of our loan book over time. Most HNW
mortgages are for owner-occupied properties, particularly
those with lower EPC ratings, where compliance with minimum
EPC requirements is less of a concern. Our top real estate
exposures primarily consist of new builds that meet the target
EPC ratings. Since the last climate risk assessment was
conducted on the March 2024 book, the composition of our top
real estate exposures may have evolved. These changes will be
reflected in the next refresh of the climate risk assessment.

Physical risk event - floods: Additionally, the increasing flood
risk associated with climate change, exacerbated by more
frequent and intense flooding events, poses further challenges.
{BP mitigates this risk through stringent lending criteria for HNW
individuals, significantly reducing default risk even when the
underlying properties are exposed to climate risks. Our credit
team assesses flood risk for all real estate transactions and
identifies appropriate mitigants for properties with elevated
exposure. Properties assessed as having high flood risk are
escalated to the Credit Committee for further review and
implementation of additional risk mitigations. The most recent
climate risk assessment focused on top HNW mortgage
exposures; future assessments will expand the scope to
include non-HNW mortgages.

Investec Bank pie Annual Financial Statements 2026

Transportation (aviation) sector

The aviation sector faces significant transition risks related to
climate change, primarily due to the difficulty in reducing
carbon emissions from jet engines, especially for long-distance
flights. These transition risks are exacerbated by rising fuel
prices, particularly for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), as well as
taxes aimed at financing carbon emission offsetting efforts and
demand management strategies. The global nature of the
aviation industry necessitates extensive policy coordination,
which may slow down the legislative process required to
decarbonise the sector.

Transition risk event — increased pricing of GHG emissions:
Transition risk may arise due to cost increases, such as taxes
on jet fuel, rising airport landing slot prices, and fines for noise
infringements. Airlines can mitigate these risks by optimising
their route offerings and scheduling in response to fines and
incentives, such as taking advantage of reduced landing fees at
certain airports.

Transition risk event ~ mandates on and regulation of existing
products and services: Tightening regulations could include
bans on ultra-short-haul flights, grounding of older aircraft that
do not meet minimum emission standards and mandatory
requirements for aircraft seating arrangements, such as
economy class only. The impact of such legislation will largely
depend on whether it is enforced in the aircraft's state of
registry or the state of operation.

Transition risk event - changing customer behaviour: Social
trends and changing consumer preferences are also influencing
the aviation sector, with an increasing adoption of SAF, albeit at
a higher cost due to limited supply. Customers are beginning to
opt for more environmentally friendly alternatives, such as train
travel. In response, many major airlines are actively investing in
SAF production facilities to enhance availability and reduce
costs over time. Despite these challenges, the demand for air
travel remains inelastic, presenting an opportunity for airlines to
adapt their strategies while still meeting consumer needs.

Energy sector

The transition narrative in the energy sector is intrinsically
linked to the technology employed. The complexities of the
energy transition, coupled with evolving government policies,
prevent us from drawing straightforward conclusions at the
asset level. For instance, while older energy plants may face
challenges, they may still be necessary for maintaining energy
capacity and grid stability.

Transition risk event — shifts in consumer preferences: We
acknowledge a global shift away from non-renewable energy
sources, with a strong move towards renewable energy
production. As part of our mitigation strategy, we view natural
gas as a transition fuel, with many combined cycle gas turbine
(CCGT) plants capable of running on hydrogen. Our largest
energy assets are strategically positioned in the UK and the
highly diversified US market. The assets in the energy and
infrastructure finance portfolio included in the most recent
climate risk assessment comprised CCGT and energy-from-
waste (EfW) plants, all located in the UK and the US. As the
scope of the climate risk assessment expands to include
additional physical hazards, geographies and exposure sizes, it
will incorporate further assets, including those in Europe.

320
06 Sustainability statement

Transition risk event ~ substitution of existing products and
services with lower emissions options: The merit order of CCGT
plants is another critical consideration. Older, non-renewable
plants are likely to rank lower in efficiency, pollution levels and
operational costs, increasing their risk of becoming stranded
assets. However, due to their relatively young profile, the
CCGTs in our top exposures are generally ranked mid to high
on the merit order, securing revenue through capacity market
agreements with counterparties.

Transition risk event ~ mandates on and regulation of existing
products and services: The introduction of carbon-related
legislation, including laws, standards and taxes that mandate
retrofitting carbon capture technology, presents both
challenges and opportunities. Our portfolio of relatively young
CCGTs positions us advantageously, as they can be retrofitted
more easily and cost-effectively, while their higher efficiency
means they are likely to emit less than older plants.

Transition risk event - uncertainty in market signals: We
recognise the dynamics in the energy-from-waste (EfW)
market, where improved landfill waste management practices
are expected to reduce waste supply to EfW plants. Despite
this, we believe the EfW market will remain competitive due to
higher landfill taxes compared to EfW gate fees.

Manufacturing sector

The transition narrative for the manufacturing sector is
intricately linked to the energy sector, particularly as the
highest carbon-emitting industries face significant transition
risks. While electrification may be a viable option for certain
sub-sectors, more energy-intensive industries, such as cement
manufacturing, are hard to abate. Manufacturing is a crucial
component of the UK economy, and recent declines in
emissions can be attributed to reduced energy intensity in
combustion-based processes and shifts in the fuel mix. To
further decarbonise the sector, it will be essential to implement
strategies such as process innovation, electrifying the energy
system and deploying carbon capture technologies at
concentrated sources.

Transition risk event — increased pricing of GHG emissions: The
dynamics of pollution permits and energy trading schemes
operating on a cap-and-trade basis for total emissions present
a key risk for IBP, as manufacturers may experience reductions
in revenue and cash flow while adjusting production levels to
comply with carbon permit limits.

Transition risk event ~ mandates on and regulation of existing
products and services: The introduction of carbon standards
and taxes could require products from high-emission industries

to meet specific carbon content or recycled content thresholds.

This shift may lead to increased costs for high-emitting
companies, particularly if these standards are enacted before
low-carbon technologies are fully developed, potentially
impacting the financial performance of our clients in these
sectors.

Transition risk event ~ costs of transition to lower emissions
technology: The role of subsidies is critical in supporting the
adoption of emerging technologies, such as green hydrogen
and post-combustion air capture. Without these subsidies,
some manufacturers could face elevated costs associated with
in-house low-carbon research and innovation, which may
hinder decarbonisation efforts. While these measures will
predominantly affect the highest-emitting industries, it is
important to note that the key risks associated with them are
largely mitigated by the composition of IBP’s manufacturing
portfolio, which primarily includes assets in industries with low
emissions intensity.

Overall findings

The overall findings from this risk assessment indicate that,
consistent with the results in 2022, the climate transition and
physical risks are low for the Bank over a 5-10-year horizon.
We have adequate capital and liquidity to operate as a going
concern while meeting regulatory capital and liquidity
requirements. This stability reinforces our confidence in the
robustness of our financial position and our ability to navigate
potential challenges in the evolving climate landscape. As we
move forward, we remain committed to refining our strategies
and enhancing our resilience in the face of climate change.

Our approach currently contains a number of uncertainties. It
depends on accurate site-level data, including geo-coordinates
and asset values, which vary in quality across the portfolio.
Additionally, further work is needed to develop a clear
methodology for differentiating between leased and owned
assets and whether to include supply chain risks for certain
companies.

Additionally, this resilience analysis was not considered during
the DMA, as the assessment was still underway at that time.

Within our own operations

We conduct physical risk assessments related to our operations
at least every three years, recognising that such evaluations are
cost-intensive and that our portfolio remains largely stable over
this period. In our latest assessment conducted in 2026, we
focused on precipitation- and temperature-related hazards,
including surface water flooding, river flooding, coastal flooding
and extreme heat. These risks were assessed using three Shared
Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs) developed by the UNFCCC".

« $SP1-2.6 represents a low-emissions scenario aligned with
strong global climate action and a 1.5-2°C warming outcome.

SSP2-4.5 reflects a middle-of-the-road scenario with
moderate transition and physical risks, resulting in a
temperature increase of approximately 2.7°C by 2100.

SSP3-~-7.0 represents a high-emissions scenario
characterised by limited climate policy action and higher
physical risk exposure, with a potential temperature increase
of approximately 3.9°C by 2100.
06 Sustainability statement

CONTINUED

For precipitation, IBP’s operating locations are projected to
experience drier summers and wetter winters, with regional
variations depending on the climate scenario. Across all
scenarios, the number of extreme precipitation days (defined
as days with more than 20mm of rainfall) is expected to
increase. Under SSP1-2.6, changes remain relatively limited
across most Investec offices. Under SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0, a
broader increase in extreme precipitation is projected, with the
majority of IBP’s offices across the UK, Europe and New York
expected to experience a moderate increase. Despite these
projections, most locations are currently assessed as having
negligible or no identifiable financial risk from coastal and fluvial
flooding.

For temperature, under SSP1-2.6, only the New York and India
offices are projected to experience more than ten additional
extreme heat days (defined as days exceeding 30°C), while UK
and European offices are expected to see minimal changes.
Under SSP2-4.5, the majority of offices are projected to
experience fewer than five additional extreme heat days
annually. Under SSP3-7.0, the trend remains relatively stable
for UK offices, while European offices may experience a slight
increase in extreme heat exposure. Overall, IBP’s offices are
assessed as having negligible or no significant financial risk
from extreme heat across all scenarios.

These changes in precipitation and temperature may impact
the health and wellbeing of our employees in certain locations.
However, the assessment confirmed that there are no material
concerns regarding the resilience of IBP’s operations. IBP
manages these risks through established operational resilience
strategies and business continuity plans, including emergency
response procedures, ensuring operational continuity.

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Current financial effects of material IROs

The Group makes use of reasonable and supportable information
to make accounting judgments and estimates related to climate
change, including the observable impacts on clients’ current
credit risk and asset valuations. Many climate change effects are
long term and inherently uncertain, having minimal influence on
accounting judgements and estimates for the current period.
Key short-term climate change impacts include:

- Expected credit loss (ECL) measurement: ECL assessments
evaluate borrowers' ability to make contractual payments as
they become due. Investec has assessed specific sectors
most vulnerable to climate risk across all jurisdictions,
focusing on clients’ capacity to meet their financing needs
and Investec’s willingness to fund these sectors. While these
assessments have not materially affected ECL, the impact on
probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and other
ECL inputs is still being determined

¢ Asset impairment and deferred tax assets: Assessments of
asset impairment, based on value in use, and the recognition
of deferred tax assets depend on future expected cash
flows. These cash flows reflect management's best estimates
of operational results, including the near-term effects of
climate risk. The Group has not made additional adjustments
to cash flows for climate risk within the considered time
frame, assuming that market indicators used for fair value
inputs already incorporate current information and insights
regarding climate risk.

EU Taxonomy

Following thorough review by IBP, IBP has decided to apply the
transitional opt-out approach permitted under the EU
Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and Commission
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 and related EU
Taxonomy transitional provisions applicable to financial
undertakings.

No activities are claimed as being associated with economic
activities that qualify as environmentally sustainable under
Articles 3 and 9 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy
Regulation).

As such, IBP has opted-out from detailed Taxonomy reporting
for the period ending 31 March 2026.

Biodiversity and ecosystems

We acknowledge that our lending and investing activities. and
to a lesser extent our own operational activities, may give rise to
negative biodiversity-related impacts. There is a clear link
between climate change (refer to our environmental policy and
climate change statement on our website} and biodiversity loss
and achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development
Goals for these go hand-in-hand. Healthy biodiversity
ecosystems create resilience that plays a key role in preventing
disturbances and disruption in the services and resources
provided to society and the markets within which our business
operate. We recognise the need to conserve biodiversity and
ecosystems, and as such adopt a precautionary approach for
sustainable management of biodiversity in all decision-making
processes, This approach supports our broader mission to
preserve biodiversity, maintain ecosystem integrity, and respect
ethical considerations in all areas of our business.

Material IROs relating to biodiversity and
ecosystems

The process for identifying and assessing material impacts,
risks and opportunities is described on page 303 and applies to
this topic.

ESRS E4: Biodiversity and ecosystems

Investec Bank pic Annual Financial Statements 2026

Biodiversity and ecosystems were assessed as material through
the Group's DMA. The assessment identified a negative impact
associated with financing activities in nature-related sectors,
which may contribute to biodiversity loss and ecosystem
degradation within the downstream value chain.

IBP’s primary interaction with biodiversity-related impacts arises
indirectly through our lending and investment activities,
particularly in sectors with dependencies on natural capital. This
approach is supported by the Group's nature and biodiversity
statement, which outlines our precautionary approach to
managing biodiversity-related risks.

In line with the transitional provisions available under ESRS E4,
IBP has applied a phased-in approach to biodiversity-related
disclosures for the current reporting period and has therefore
not provided detailed disclosures under ESRS E4.

IBP will continue to monitor biodiversity-related opportunities,
risks and impacts and further develop its approach in line with
evolving regulatory expectations, including integration into
existing environmental and risk management frameworks where
appropriate.

Group nature and biodiversity statement

The Group’s nature and biodiversity statement outlines a
precautionary approach to managing biodiversity-related risks,
including integrating biodiversity considerations into lending and
investment decisions, applying enhanced sustainability screening
for high-risk activities, and avoiding financing activities that may
have significant adverse impacts on ecosystems.

Actions and performance

We manage biodiversity-related impacts through the integration
of biodiversity considerations into its existing environmental and
risk management processes. This includes the application of
sustainability screening for high-risk activities, consideration of
biodiversity impacts in lending and investment decisions, and
ongoing monitoring through established governance and risk
oversight structures.

Metrics and targets

We do not currently apply quantitative metrics to measure
biodiversity-related impacts, reflecting the early stage of
development in methodologies, data availability and industry
practice in this area. The Group will continue to monitor
developments and assess the feasibility of introducing
appropriate metrics over time.

Our people

Our purpose of creating enduring worth underpins how we
shape strategy and deliver long-term value for our
stakeholders. It informs the environment we create for our
people— one that shows deep respect for individuals, prizes
inclusion and enables Out of the Ordinary performance. We
achieve this through organisational values and core
philosophies that guide our conduct and behaviour.

Our people are central to delivering on this purpose. Our
employee value proposition positions our culture at the core of
the organisation. Guided by our purpose and strengthened by
our values, our culture is defined by material ownership,
freedom to operate with accountability and open and honest
dialogue. We challenge convention with conviction, prize
inclusion and practice a generosity of spirit with deep care. This
is our strategic differentiator and competitive advantage — it is
how we deliver performance to all our stakeholders.

and governance outcomes. These initiatives contribute to a
diverse and inclusive workforce, strengthened governance, and
a supportive working environment that promotes physical,
mental, emotional and financial wellbeing.

At the same time, we recognise a financial risk associated with
